title: Heat and temperature: why the same heat warms oil faster than water

summary.text: Stand a tumbler of cooking oil and a tumbler of water in the same bath of hot water, and the oil warms up about twice as fast. Pour hot water at 60 degrees over ice in a small katori, and it melts less ice than a big bowl of water at only 40 degrees. Your child measures both with a thermometer. They find that temperature says how hot a thing is, while the heat it can give depends on how much of it there is and what it is made of. Then they follow heat into melting ice, a balloon on a bottle, a wet cloth and a burning groundnut.
summary.art: Two steel tumblers standing in a pan of hot water, one holding golden oil and one holding clear water, each with a thermometer, and the oil thermometer reading higher.

intro.hook: Two steel tumblers stand in the same pan of hot water. One holds a katori of cooking oil and the other a katori of water. Both started at room temperature. After ten minutes, one of them has warmed far more than the other. Which one, do you think? And why?
intro.text: The pan gives the same heat to both tumblers, yet they do not end up the same. In this unit you test this with two thermometers. You find out why a small cup of hot water can melt less ice than a big bowl of warm water. You watch a thermometer stay still while ice melts, though heat keeps going in. You blow up a balloon with warm air, cool a thermometer with a wet cloth, and measure the heat in a groundnut.
intro.art: A child with a notebook looking at two thermometers standing in two tumblers in a pan of hot water, with a question mark above the tumblers.

outcomes: I can explain that temperature tells how hot a thing is, while the heat it can give depends on how much of it there is and what it is made of.
I can say that the same heat warms different materials by different amounts, and that water needs more heat than oil, sand or metal to warm by one degree.
I can use thermometers in a fair test to compare how fast two materials warm up, and read the result from a table and a graph.
I can predict which of two amounts of water can melt more ice, and give a reason.
I can explain why the temperature stays still while ice melts or water boils, though heat keeps going in.
I can give three ways to make heat from movement, and say that most things grow bigger when they get warm.
I can explain how sweat and a wet cloth cool us, and why seas and our bodies change temperature slowly.
I can tell how Joseph Black showed that temperature and the amount of heat are different things.

terms.meaning: The total movement energy of all the tiny particles in a thing. A bigger thing at the same temperature has more thermal energy.
terms.example: A bucket of water at 40 degrees has far more thermal energy than a katori of water at 40 degrees.
terms.art: A bucket and a katori of water side by side, each with a thermometer reading 40, and a label saying the bucket holds more.

terms.meaning: Thermal energy that moves from a warmer thing to a cooler thing.
terms.example: When you hold a hot tumbler, heat moves from the tumbler into your hands.
terms.art: A hot tumbler in a child's hands with a red arrow pointing from the tumbler into the hands.

terms.meaning: How hot or cold a thing is. It tells how fast the particles jiggle, on average.
terms.example: A thermometer in a cup of tea reads 65 degrees Celsius.
terms.art: A thermometer standing in a steel cup of tea with the line at 65.

terms.meaning: A unit of heat. One calorie is the heat that warms 1 gram of water by 1 degree Celsius. It is about 4.2 joules.
terms.example: To warm 100 grams of water by 10 degrees you need 1,000 calories.
terms.art: A tiny katori of water with a thermometer rising by one degree and a label saying one calorie for each gram.

terms.meaning: 1,000 calories. It is the unit on food packets. People often write it as Calorie with a capital C, or as kcal.
terms.example: A medium chapati has about 100 kilocalories, enough to warm a litre of water from 28 degrees to boiling.
terms.art: A chapati on a plate beside a litre bottle of water with a number 100 kcal between them.

terms.meaning: The scientist's unit for energy, and so for heat too. One calorie is about 4.2 joules.
terms.example: Heating a cup of tea (150 grams) from 28 to 70 degrees takes about 26,000 joules.
terms.art: A cup of tea with steam and a tag that says 26,000 joules.

terms.meaning: The heat needed to warm 1 gram of a material by 1 degree Celsius. Each material has its own number.
terms.example: Water needs 1 calorie. Cooking oil needs about half a calorie. Steel needs about a tenth of a calorie.
terms.art: Three small piles labelled water, oil and steel, with numbers 1, one half and one tenth on cards.

terms.meaning: A thing that holds a lot of heat, so it warms and cools slowly.
terms.example: A hot water bottle is a heat store. It keeps a bed warm for hours.
terms.art: A hot water bottle under a blanket with warm orange glow lines around it.

terms.meaning: The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid. For ice it is 0 degrees Celsius.
terms.example: Ice in a glass of water stays at 0 degrees until the last piece has melted.
terms.art: An ice cube melting in a glass with a thermometer reading 0.

terms.meaning: The temperature at which a liquid boils. For water at sea level it is 100 degrees Celsius.
terms.example: Water in an open pot stays at 100 degrees however high the flame is.
terms.art: A pot of boiling water on a stove with a thermometer reading 100 and a big flame under it.

terms.meaning: The heat that goes into melting, boiling or evaporating something. The temperature stays still while it goes in. Latent means hidden.
terms.example: Melting 1 gram of ice takes 80 calories, with no change in temperature.
terms.art: A block of ice on a heater plate with a flat thermometer and arrows going into the ice.

terms.meaning: A liquid slowly turning into a gas from its surface, at any temperature. The fastest particles leave first.
terms.example: Wet clothes dry on a line because their water evaporates.
terms.art: A wet shirt on a washing line with tiny water particles rising from it.

terms.meaning: To take up less space. Most things contract when they cool down.
terms.example: A balloon shrinks when you put it in the fridge, because the air inside contracts.
terms.art: A balloon big on the left in warm air and small on the right in a fridge.

terms.meaning: When two things that touch are at the same temperature, so no heat moves between them.
terms.example: A thermometer in a tumbler of water stops rising when it reaches the water's temperature.
terms.art: A thermometer in a tumbler with the red line stopped, and a label saying same temperature.

terms.meaning: The usual weather of a place over many years.
terms.example: Chennai has a warm, humid climate. Jaisalmer has a hot, dry one.
terms.art: Two small maps of India, one with a coast city and one with a desert city, with weather symbols.

terms.meaning: The coldest temperature that is possible, about minus 273 degrees Celsius. Particles move as little as the rules of nature allow.
terms.example: Scientists in laboratories have cooled things to a tiny fraction of a degree above absolute zero.
terms.art: A thermometer scale going down to a line at the very bottom marked absolute zero.

terms.meaning: Salty water that skin lets out when the body is too warm. When it evaporates, it takes heat from the skin.
terms.example: After a long run, your skin is wet with sweat, and the breeze feels cool.
terms.art: A child's face with drops of sweat and a small fan blowing from the side.

terms.meaning: To slow down the movement of heat, for example with a cloth, a lid or a layer of air.
terms.example: A lid on a pot of dal keeps the dal hot for longer.
terms.art: A steel pot with a lid, with arrows of heat stopped at the lid.

explanations.concept: Temperature and heat are different things
explanations.definition: Temperature tells how fast the particles of a thing jiggle, on average. Heat is the thermal energy that moves from a warmer thing to a cooler thing.
explanations.description: A katori of tea and a bucket of tea can have the same temperature. Their particles jiggle equally fast on average. But the bucket has far more particles, so it holds far more thermal energy, and it can give away far more heat. A thermometer cannot tell you this. It only tells you how hot a thing is, and so which way heat will go. To know how much heat a thing can give, you must also know how much of it there is, and what it is made of.
examples: A spark from a sparkler is hotter than boiling water, but it hardly warms your hand, because it holds almost no heat.
A bucket of bath water at 40 degrees can warm you more than a cup of tea at 70 degrees, because it holds far more heat.
A big pot of rasam stays hot for much longer than a small bowl of it at the same temperature.
explanations.art: A katori and a bucket of water, both with thermometers reading 40, and many small particles drawn inside the bucket for each one in the katori.

explanations.concept: Measuring heat: the calorie and the joule
explanations.definition: A calorie is the heat that warms 1 gram of water by 1 degree Celsius. It is about 4.2 joules. A kilocalorie is 1,000 calories.
explanations.description: Heat is energy, so we measure it in the same units as energy. Scientists use the joule. An older unit, the calorie, is easier to picture, because it is defined with water. To warm 100 grams of water by 10 degrees, you need 100 times 10, which is 1,000 calories. The Calories on a food packet are really kilocalories. One kilocalorie warms a litre of water by 1 degree. A medium chapati has about 100 kilocalories. In theory, that is enough heat to take a litre of water from 28 degrees to boiling.
examples: Warming a cup of tea (150 grams) from 28 to 70 degrees takes 150 times 42, which is 6,300 calories, or about 6 kilocalories.
An adult eats about 2,000 kilocalories a day, as much heat as it takes to warm 2,000 litres of water by 1 degree.
One calorie is about 4.2 joules, so the cup of tea needs about 26,000 joules.
explanations.art: A litre bottle of water with a thermometer, and a chapati beside it with an arrow labelled 100 kilocalories.

explanations.concept: How much heat it takes: amount, material and change
explanations.definition: The heat needed to warm a thing depends on three things: how much of it there is, what it is made of, and how many degrees you want to warm it.
explanations.description: In calories, heat needed is the mass in grams, times the specific heat of the material, times the number of degrees. Water has a specific heat of 1. Cooking oil has about one half. Dry sand and aluminium have about one fifth. Steel has about one tenth. So to warm 200 grams of water by 30 degrees you need 200 times 1 times 30, which is 6,000 calories. For 200 grams of oil you need about half as much, 3,000 calories. The same heat will warm the oil by about twice as many degrees. This is what the oil and water test shows.
examples: A steel spoon heats up very fast in a hot pan, because steel needs only about a tenth of a calorie for each gram and each degree.
A brick wall takes a long time to warm in the sun and to cool at night, because a brick wall has a lot of mass.
A gold bangle needs very little heat to warm up, because gold needs only about 0.03 of a calorie for each gram and each degree.
explanations.art: A table with five materials in a row (water, oil, sand, steel, gold) and bars for their specific heats, with water the tallest.

explanations.concept: Why water holds so much heat
explanations.definition: Water needs more heat for each degree than almost any common material. The reason is partly how its particles are built and joined.
explanations.description: Heat does not only make particles move faster. In water, a good part of the heat goes into making the particles spin, wobble and stretch the links that hold them together. That heat does not show up as speed, so the thermometer rises less. Scientists understand this in general. Working out the exact number for water from first principles is still hard. Water is odd in dozens of ways, and scientists are still working out the reasons for some of them. We call this an idea, not a finished answer.
examples: Water takes about twice as much heat as oil to warm by the same amount.
Water takes more than eight times as much heat as steel, gram for gram.
Ice takes only about half as much heat as liquid water to warm by one degree.
explanations.art: A close-up of water particles shaped like tiny boomerangs, with arrows for moving, spinning and wobbling, and a small thermometer beside them.

perspectives.explanation: The links between water particles, called hydrogen bonds, take in a lot of heat as they stretch and bend. This is a big part of why water holds so much heat.
The links are only part of the story. Water's particles can also store heat as spin and wobble, and quantum rules decide how much each way takes. The full numbers are still being worked out.

explanations.concept: Sea, sand and sky: why places warm differently
explanations.definition: Land warms and cools faster than the sea. This is because water needs more heat for each degree, and because sunlight and waves spread heat through deep water.
explanations.description: In the sun, dry sand needs only about a fifth of the heat that water needs for each degree. Sunlight stays at the sand surface, so the top layer gets very hot. In the sea, sunlight goes down several metres, and waves and currents mix the heat through a deep layer. So the sea warms slowly by day and cools slowly by night. Places by the sea, such as Chennai, Kochi and Mumbai, usually have only 8 to 10 degrees between their day and night. In a desert, such as Jaisalmer, the day and night can differ by 15 degrees or more. The difference in warming between land and sea also helps to drive the monsoon winds.
examples: The sand at Marina beach in Chennai burns your feet at noon, while the sea beside it feels cool.
Desert nights are cold because dry sand and thin dry air hold little heat and give it up quickly.
The sea along India's coast keeps the weather milder than far inland, all year round.

In 1856, Eunice Foote, an American scientist, is reported to have put thermometers in glass tubes of different gases in the sunshine. The tubes warmed by different amounts, which is the same idea as sand and water warming differently.
explanations.art: A map of India with a coast city and a desert city, and two small graphs of day and night temperature, flat for the coast and steep for the desert.

explanations.concept: Sharing heat: where a mixture ends up
explanations.definition: When you mix two amounts of the same liquid at different temperatures, the mix ends between them, nearer the temperature of the bigger amount.
explanations.description: A mix of 1 litre at 80 degrees and 3 litres at 20 degrees: multiply each amount by its temperature, add, and divide by the total. 1 times 80 is 80. 3 times 20 is 60. 80 plus 60 is 140. Divide by 4 litres and you get 35 degrees. The 3 litres are three times as much, so the mix is three times closer to 20 than to 80. For different materials you must also include their specific heats. A hot steel spoon dropped into a cup of cool water warms the water by only about 2 degrees, because the spoon holds very little heat for each degree.
examples: A little hot milk in a big glass of cold milk warms it only a little.
A bucket of bath water is mixed from a kettle of hot water and a lot of cold water.
A hot idli steamer plate dropped into a basin of water warms the water by a few degrees.
explanations.art: A jug of hot water and a bigger jug of cold water pouring into a bucket, with three numbers on the thermometers: 80, 20 and 35.

explanations.concept: Heat in, but no change in temperature: melting and boiling
explanations.definition: While ice melts or water boils, heat keeps going in but the temperature stays still. The heat is used to pull the particles apart.
explanations.description: Melting 1 gram of ice takes about 80 calories, as much heat as it takes to warm 1 gram of water by 80 degrees. Boiling 1 gram of water away takes about 540 calories. All that time, the thermometer sits at 0 degrees for melting ice and at 100 degrees for boiling water at sea level. The heat is not lost. It breaks the links between the particles. Scientists call it latent heat, which means hidden heat. This is why ice cools a drink so well, and why steam burns so badly.
examples: A glass of lassi with ice stays near 0 degrees at the ice, until all the ice has melted.
A pot of water on a high flame boils faster, but its temperature stays at about 100 degrees.
Steam at 100 degrees burns your skin worse than water at 100 degrees, because the steam gives out all its hidden heat as it turns back to water.
explanations.art: A line graph of temperature against time with a flat piece at 0 and another flat piece at 100, and arrows for heat going in all the time.

explanations.definition: Rubbing, bending, hammering and squashing all make heat, because movement energy turns into the jiggling of particles.
explanations.description: Rub your palms and they get warm. Bend a wire back and forth and the bend gets warm. Squash the air in a bicycle pump and the pump gets warm. In each case, a push moved something, and the movement energy ended up as heat. In the 1840s, James Joule showed that the same amount of movement always makes the same amount of heat. He let falling weights turn a paddle in water and measured how much the water warmed. His numbers gave about 4.2 joules for each calorie, which is the number we still use. This is also why friction makes things warm.
examples: Matchsticks light when you rub the head against the box.
The brake blocks of a bicycle get warm when you brake hard.
A meteor glows as it falls into the air, because the air in front of it is squashed so hard that it becomes very hot.
explanations.art: A paddle wheel in a jar of water turned by a weight on a string, with a thermometer in the water.

explanations.concept: Things grow bigger when they are warm
explanations.definition: Most things expand when they are warmed and contract when they are cooled. Gases expand the most, liquids less, solids the least.
explanations.description: Warm air in a closed bottle pushes out more strongly. Air grows by about 1 part in 270 for each degree. Over 30 degrees that is about 11 parts in 100. Liquids grow far less. Solids grow least of all. A 100-metre steel bridge grows about 4 centimetres when it warms by 30 degrees. That is why bridges and railway tracks have small gaps. In India, blacksmiths fitted iron tyres on wooden cart wheels by heating the tyre until it grew a little, slipping it on, and cooling it with water. As it shrank, it gripped the wheel tight. Water is odd. It shrinks as it cools down to about 4 degrees, then expands again as it freezes.
examples: A stuck metal jar lid often comes loose in hot water, because the metal lid grows more than the glass jar.
Overhead power lines hang lower on a hot day, because the wire has grown longer.
A thick glass of cold water can crack if you pour boiling water in, because the inside grows before the outside.
explanations.art: A railway track with a small gap between two rails, and a thermometer reading 40 in the sun.

explanations.definition: When a liquid evaporates, the fastest particles leave the surface. The particles left behind move more slowly on average, so the liquid cools.
explanations.description: Water particles at the surface move at very different speeds. The fastest ones have enough energy to escape into the air. They carry their energy away with them. What stays behind is cooler. Evaporating 1 gram of water takes more than 500 calories from whatever it leaves. That is why sweat cools you, why a wet cloth feels cold, and why water in a clay matka stays cooler than the air. On a humid day, such as in Chennai or Kolkata in the rainy season, the air is already full of water, so sweat evaporates slowly and you feel hotter.
examples: Coming out of a bath, you feel cold until you dry, because the water on your skin is evaporating.
Water in a clay matka stays cooler than the air, because some water seeps through the clay and evaporates from the outside.
Dogs pant, and elephants flap their wet ears, to lose heat by evaporation.
explanations.art: A clay matka with tiny water drops seeping through its wall and arrows of heat leaving with the evaporating water.

explanations.concept: A body that stays at 37 degrees
explanations.definition: Humans and other mammals and birds keep their insides at a nearly steady temperature by making heat and getting rid of it at just the right rate.
explanations.description: Your body makes heat all the time from food. When you are too warm, your skin widens its blood vessels, so more heat leaves, and you sweat. When you are too cold, you shiver, because shivering muscles make extra heat. A fever is the body setting a higher target for a while. Your body is about 60 to 70 parts in 100 water, and water holds so much heat that your temperature changes slowly. A lizard has no such inside heater. She warms on a sunny rock, and cools in the shade. Most living beings are somewhere between the two.
examples: A crowded room warms up, because every person gives out heat.
Children shiver when they come out of the sea, because their muscles make heat to keep the body warm.
A hen's body is about 41 degrees, warmer than yours.
explanations.art: A child with thermometer reading 37, a hen reading 41 and a lizard on a rock, with arrows for heat in and out.

explanations.definition: Absolute zero, about minus 273 degrees Celsius, is the coldest temperature possible. Nobody knows if there is a hottest temperature.
explanations.description: As things cool, their particles move less. At absolute zero they would move as little as the rules of nature allow. They do not stop completely, because quantum physics says some small movement always remains. No one can reach absolute zero exactly, but laboratories have come within a billionth of a degree. At the other end, the centre of the Sun is about 15 million degrees. In particle accelerators, scientists have made a tiny blob of matter that was reported to reach several trillion degrees for a moment. Is there a top limit? That is still an open question.
examples: The Boomerang Nebula, a cloud of gas in space, is reported to be the coldest natural place known, at about minus 272 degrees Celsius.
The centre of the Sun is about 15 million degrees Celsius.
Scientists have cooled atoms to less than a billionth of a degree above absolute zero in some laboratories.
explanations.art: A tall thermometer scale from absolute zero at the bottom to the centre of the Sun at the top, with a question mark above.

perspectives.explanation: There is probably no hottest temperature in principle, but near a value called the Planck temperature our known laws of physics stop working. So we cannot say what happens there.
Hot and cold are not mirror images. Cold has a floor, but heat may have a ceiling set by a deeper theory of gravity and quantum physics that nobody has yet.

agreed.text: The heat needed to warm a thing equals its mass, times its specific heat, times the change in temperature.
agreed.evidence: Heat has been measured in careful experiments since the 1760s, by warming known masses of many materials. The numbers agree every time. Our oil and water test is a small version.

agreed.text: Water takes more heat than almost any common material to warm by one degree.
agreed.evidence: Tables of specific heats, measured in laboratories around the world, list water near the top. This is why seas warm and cool slowly and steady the weather of coasts.

agreed.text: While a solid melts or a liquid boils, heat goes in but the temperature stays still.
agreed.evidence: A thermometer in melting ice stays at 0 degrees until the last ice has gone. A thermometer in an open pot of boiling water stays at about 100 degrees at sea level.

agreed.text: Movement energy can turn into heat, and the exchange rate is fixed: about 4.2 joules for each calorie.
agreed.evidence: James Joule measured it in the 1840s, with paddles driven by falling weights. Many careful measurements since then have found the same number.

agreed.text: Most solids, liquids and gases expand when they are warmed and contract when they are cooled.
agreed.evidence: This is how liquid thermometers work. It is also why bridges and railways are built with small gaps.

agreed.text: When a liquid evaporates, the liquid left behind is cooler.
agreed.evidence: A thermometer wrapped in wet cloth reads lower than a dry one in the same air. Sweat cools us in the same way.

challenging.claim: A thermometer reading tells you how much heat a thing holds.
challenging.who: Many people, and scientists before the 1760s.
challenging.for: A hotter thing usually feels as though it has more heat, and a thermometer is how we measure it.
challenging.against: A bucket of bath water at 40 degrees holds far more heat than a cup of tea at 70 degrees. Joseph Black showed in the 1760s that temperature and the amount of heat are different things.

challenging.claim: If you turn up the flame under a pot of boiling water, the water gets hotter.
challenging.for: A bigger flame puts in more heat, and more heat usually means a higher temperature.
challenging.against: In an open pot, boiling water stays at about 100 degrees whatever the flame. The extra heat makes the water boil away faster. To make it hotter, you must stop it boiling, as a pressure cooker does.

challenging.claim: Sweat cools us because sweat is cold.
challenging.for: Sweat feels cold on the skin, and a cold hand cools a warm cheek.
challenging.against: Sweat starts at the temperature of the body. It cools you by evaporating, which takes heat from your skin. On a humid day, sweat evaporates slowly, so it cools you less.

challenging.claim: Land and sea warm differently because the sun shines harder on the land.
challenging.for: Sand feels far hotter than the sea at noon.
challenging.against: The sun shines about equally on both. The sea warms less because water needs more heat for each degree and because sunlight and waves spread the heat through deep water.

challenging.claim: A hot thing weighs more because heat is a substance with weight.
challenging.who: Many scientists in the 1700s, who thought of heat as a fluid.
challenging.for: Heat seemed to flow from one thing into another, like water from a jug.
challenging.against: Careful weighing found no gain in weight. Today we know that energy has a tiny mass, but it is far too little to weigh. A litre of water heated by 100 degrees gains only a few trillionths of a kilogram.

challenging.claim: At absolute zero, nothing moves at all.
challenging.who: Many people, and some older textbooks.
challenging.for: As particles cool they move less and less, so it seems they would stop completely.
challenging.against: Quantum physics says particles keep a small amount of movement even at absolute zero. Scientists call it zero-point motion, and it has effects that can be measured.

big_questions.q: The oil and the water sat in the same bath, and the oil ended up hotter. What does a thermometer tell you about the heat that went in, and what does it not tell you?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you needed to know besides the temperature to say how much heat a thing had taken in.

big_questions.q: A sparkler's spark is hotter than boiling water, but it hardly hurts. What else besides temperature decides whether something can burn you?
big_questions.hint: Think about the bucket and the katori. Which one could melt more ice?

big_questions.q: While ice melts, heat keeps going in, but the thermometer stays at 0. Where does that heat go?
big_questions.hint: Think about what has to happen to the particles in a solid before they can flow as a liquid.

big_questions.q: Your body is mostly water and stays near 37 degrees whether the day is hot or cool. How much of that is the water, and how much is your body working?
big_questions.hint: Think about sweating, shivering and the way a pot of water warms slowly.

big_questions.q: The sea warms and cools slowly, so places by the sea have gentler weather. How might that shape where people live, what they grow and how they build?
big_questions.hint: Think about Chennai, Kochi and the Thar desert. Where would you want to live in summer? In winter?

big_questions.q: If heat is the jiggling of particles, could you make a tumbler of water hotter by shaking it for a long time? Why does it hardly warm?
big_questions.hint: Think about how much movement energy your arms give the water, and how much heat water needs for each degree.

big_questions.q: There is a coldest possible temperature, but nobody knows if there is a hottest. Why might hot and cold not be mirror images of each other?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens to particles as they slow down, and what would have to happen for them to speed up for ever.

big_questions.q: Every fridge and air conditioner moves heat out of one place and into another. If a million of them run in a city at once, where does all the heat go?
big_questions.hint: Think about the warm grille at the back of a fridge, and about streets and rooftops in a hot city.

big_questions.q: A hot thing and a cold thing end up at one temperature, but their particles never stop jiggling. So when 'nothing is happening', what is still going on?
big_questions.hint: Think about particles bumping into each other, passing energy one way and the other, in a balance.

story.title: The Drums on the Cold Night
story.note: A made-up story. Meera, her family and their shed are imagined. The science is true: water holds much more heat for each degree than air, so drums of water soak up the sun's heat by day and give it back slowly at night. On cold January nights, frost can settle in the high valleys near Munnar. In real life, drums of water can keep a small closed shed a few degrees warmer, but they could not protect an open field.
text: Meera lived on a hillside above Munnar, in Kerala. Tea bushes covered the slopes like a green carpet. Every morning the mist was so thick that the tea pluckers walked into it and disappeared.

Her family did not work on a tea estate. They had a small plot behind the house, with a shed roofed in clear plastic. Inside the shed, her mother Sreedevi grew tomatoes and beans for the Sunday market. The shed was her pride.

One January morning, the radio said that a cold wave was coming. Tonight would be the coldest night in years. Meera knew what that meant. On such nights, frost settled on the grass in the high valleys. One touch of frost could kill every tomato flower in the shed.

Her uncle Gopan had just come home after working for years in the Gulf. He was proud of how much he knew. At noon he marched into the shed with a bucket of glowing charcoal. 'We will warm the air,' he said. 'Charcoal is hot.'

Ammamma, Meera's grandmother, caught his sleeve. 'Burning charcoal in a closed shed?' she said. 'The smoke will put every one of us to sleep. Take it out.' Gopan set the bucket down outside and rubbed the back of his neck.
'Then what do we do?' he asked. 'There is no power for a heater, and the cold is coming.' Nobody answered. Sreedevi looked at her tomato plants and said nothing.
Meera was thinking about last week at school. Her teacher, Lathika Teacher, had given the class a puzzle. Why does oil in the kadai get hot almost at once, while the water for tea takes so long?

The class had tested it. A tumbler of oil and a tumbler of water stood in the same bath of hot water. The oil warmed up twice as fast. 'Water needs a lot of heat to warm up,' Lathika Teacher had said. 'So when water cools down, it gives a lot of heat back.' Meera had copied this into her notebook in her best handwriting.
In the corner of the shed stood three old blue drums, where Amma kept rainwater. Meera counted them. 'Uncle,' she said, 'please fill the drums with water.'
Gopan laughed. 'Water? Child, water is the coldest thing in this shed.'

'Water is not cold,' said Meera. 'Water just takes a lot of heat to change. The sun has been on this shed all day. If we fill the drums, they will soak up the sun's heat. Tonight, when the air gets cold, the drums will give it back slowly.'
'Where did you learn this?' asked Gopan. 'From a tumbler of oil,' said Meera.
Gopan did not believe her. But the sky was turning grey, and nobody else had an idea. So he picked up the buckets, and they filled the three drums from the rain tank, one bucket after another.
By six in the evening, the shed was warm and damp. Meera hung her school thermometer from a beam inside. Gopan hung a second one outside, on a nail. Inside it read 24. Outside it read 9.

They sat up with a lantern and a flask of tea. At nine o'clock the shed read 16. At midnight it read 11. Outside, the nail thermometer showed 4, and then 2. 'It is falling,' said Gopan. 'Of course it is,' said Meera. 'The shed is losing heat to the sky. But look how slowly.'

At three in the morning, the thermometer outside read 1. The grass was white, and the air stung their noses. Inside the shed it read 8. Gopan put his hand on the nearest drum. 'It is warm,' he whispered. 'How can it still be warm?'

'It has a lot to give,' said Meera. 'One drum of water holds as much heat for every degree as the air of fifteen sheds. It cannot give it all away in one night.' She had worked out the sum on the back of her notebook.

In the morning, the whole valley was white. Rajan Chettan next door had left his beans in the open. Their leaves hung black and soft, like wet cloth. In Sreedevi's shed, the tomato flowers were yellow and fresh. A few leaf tips were nipped, and that was all.
Gopan walked round the shed twice. Then he sat on an upturned bucket. 'Meera,' he said, 'explain it to me again. Slowly this time. I want to tell the men at the tea shop.'
Meera opened her notebook. She drew the sun, the drums and the cold night. Under the picture she wrote: Water is slow to warm and slow to cool. The drums store the sun's heat.
Sreedevi, listening from the door, added a warning. 'Three drums can keep a small closed shed above freezing. They could not save a whole field under the open sky. The sky takes heat away too fast.'

'A field would need far more water,' said Meera, 'and a roof.' That evening Ammamma tucked a hot steel bottle into Meera's blanket. 'Your great-grandmother knew this too,' she said. 'She never needed a thermometer.'
story.epiphany: Water takes a lot of heat to warm up, so it also gives out a lot of heat as it cools. Drums of water soak up the day's warmth and give it back slowly through the night.
ask: Why did Meera fill the drums with water, when water feels cold?
Why would three drums of oil have kept the shed less warm than three drums of water?
Why can drums of water help a small closed shed, but not a whole open field?
Where did the heat in the drums come from in the afternoon, and where had it gone by morning?
