games.title: Heat Bank: which one needs more heat?
games.context: This is a card game about how much heat different things hold. Each card shows a thing at home, and on the back, how much heat it takes to warm it by one degree. Players guess which of two cards holds more.

printables.title: 24 thing cards to cut out (the thing on the front, the heat it takes to warm it by one degree on the back)

items.f: A cup of cooking oil, 200 grams
A katori of dry sand, 150 grams
A bucket of dry sand, 10 kilograms
The air in a small room, 36 kilograms
A bottle of coconut water, 1 kilogram
A pressure cooker pot of dal, 3 kilograms

items.b: less than 1 calorie for each degree

printables.title: 8 question cards to cut out (the question on the front, the answer on the back)

items.f: The same heat goes into a cup of water and a cup of oil of the same mass. Which warms by more degrees?
items.b: The oil. It needs only about half as much heat for each degree.
Heat. It is the heat that warms 1 gram of water by 1 degree Celsius.

items.f: A bucket of water and a cup of tea are both at 40 degrees. Which can give away more heat?
items.b: The bucket. It has far more water, so it holds far more heat.

items.f: Why does a steel spoon get hot so fast in a hot pan?
items.b: Steel needs only about a tenth as much heat as water for each degree and each gram.

items.f: Ice melts in warm water, but the thermometer in the ice reads 0. Where does the heat go?
items.b: Into pulling the ice particles apart, so the ice can turn to water.

items.f: A pot of water and a pot of iron of the same mass start at the same temperature and cool in a room. Which cools more slowly?
items.b: The water. It holds more heat for each degree.

items.f: How many calories are in one kilocalorie?
Why do towns by the sea have smaller swings between day and night than desert towns?
items.b: The sea holds a lot of heat, so it warms and cools slowly and steadies the air.

setup.art: Two piles of cut-out cards on a table, thing cards in one and question cards in the other, with a pencil and a score sheet beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards. Make a pile of thing cards and a pile of question cards.

setup.art: Two thing cards side by side, face up on the thing side, with a child pointing at one and saying a guess.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over two thing cards. Guess which needs more heat to warm by one degree.

setup.art: The same two cards turned over to show their numbers, and a player writing points on the score sheet.
setup.caption: 3. Check the backs of the cards. Score your points.

rules: Make one pile of the 24 thing cards, with the thing side up. Make a second pile of the 8 question cards, with the question side up.
On your turn, take the top two thing cards and put them side by side. Do not turn them over yet.
Say which card you think needs more heat to warm by one degree, and why. This is your first guess.
Then say which one would warm by more degrees if each got the same heat, for example 1,000 calories. This is your second guess.
Turn both cards over to check. A right first guess scores 1 point. A right second guess scores 1 point. The second guess is always the card with the smaller number.
Then take the top question card. Another player reads it out, you answer, and they turn it over to check. A right answer scores 1 point. If you play alone, check it yourself.
Play until all 24 thing cards are used. That is 12 turns. With 2 players, each has 6 turns. With 4 players, each has 3.
The most points wins. Then everyone works together. Lay all 24 thing cards in one line, from the smallest heat per degree to the largest, and turn them over to check.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 thing cards and the 8 question cards. Make one pile of each. Give each player a pencil and a score sheet.
flow.say: Each thing card shows something from home, and how much heat it takes to warm it by one degree. We will guess which of two things takes more heat.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Make two piles. Get a pencil and a score sheet.
flow.parent: Read out the number on one card as an example: a cup of water takes 200 calories for each degree. Remind your child that a calorie is the heat that warms 1 gram of water by 1 degree.
flow.context: This is the first step of Heat Bank. You set up the cards and the score sheet.

flow.do: Play one practice turn with the card 'A cup of water' and the card 'A steel spoon'. Make the two guesses, turn the cards over, and score them.
flow.say: Practice turn. A cup of water, and a steel spoon. Which needs more heat to warm by one degree? Which warms by more degrees from the same heat?
flow.kid: Practice turn. A cup of water and a steel spoon. Which needs more heat?

check.q: A cup of water takes 200 calories for each degree, and a steel spoon takes about 4. If each gets 100 calories, which warms by more degrees?
options: The steel spoon
The cup of water
Both warm by the same number of degrees
check.why: The spoon needs far less heat for each degree, so the same heat warms it far more. Picking the cup of water is common, because water feels like it heats quickly. But water needs a lot of heat for each degree.

flow.context: In this step, you play one practice turn and learn how to score.

flow.do: Play the game. After each thing turn, take a question card.
flow.say: Your turn. Take two cards. Which needs more heat to warm by one degree? Why do you think so? Which would warm by more degrees from the same heat?
flow.kid: Take two cards. Which needs more heat for each degree? Why?

ask.q: Why does a bucket of water need so much more heat than a cup of water?
good: It has far more water to warm.
There are many more particles to speed up.

flow.parent: Surprises children enjoy: a baby's body needs far more heat for each degree than a bucket of dry sand. The air of a small room needs about as much as a bucket of water. A gold bangle needs almost nothing.
flow.context: In this step, you play the main game and score points.

flow.do: Lay all 24 thing cards in one line, from the smallest number to the largest. Turn them over to check the order.
flow.say: Now let's make one long line from the smallest heat per degree to the largest. Where does your own body go? Where does the air in a room go?
flow.kid: Make one line. Smallest number first. Check your order.

check.q: Which of these needs the most heat to warm by one degree?
options: A steel spoon
A bucket of water
A gold bangle
check.why: The bucket holds so much water that it needs 10,000 calories for each degree. A steel spoon needs about 4, and a gold bangle less than 1. Amount matters as well as material.

flow.context: In this step, you put the cards in order of heat per degree.

flow.do: Look back at the line of cards together.
flow.say: Which cards are made of a lot of material? Which are made of a material that holds a lot of heat? Which are both?
flow.kid: Which things are big? Which hold a lot of heat for their size?
flow.think: A child's body needs about three times as much heat per degree as the air in a small room. What does that tell you about why your body stays warm?
flow.context: This is the last step of Heat Bank.

experiments.title: Oil and Water in a Warm Bath: which warms faster?
experiments.question: If a tumbler of cooking oil and a tumbler of water stand in the same hot bath, which one warms up more in 12 minutes, and by how much?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which will warm up more, the oil or the water? Will the difference be small or big? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two tumblers of the same size and metal. Put 100 millilitres of oil in one and 100 millilitres of water in the other. Both must start at room temperature. Stand them side by side in the same bath. Stir gently before every reading, and read both at the same times. Only the liquid changes, so any difference comes from the liquid.

materials.item: two laboratory thermometers that read from about minus 10 to 110 °C, or two digital kitchen probes. A fever thermometer will not work, because it reads only from about 32 to 42 °C. Only one thermometer? Do the test twice, oil first and water second, with a fresh bath at the same temperature.
two steel tumblers of the same size and shape
100 millilitres of cooking oil, such as groundnut or sunflower oil
100 millilitres of tap water, measured with the same cup, which should be marked in millilitres
a wide pan or basin, and a kettle or pot of boiling water for a grown-up to use
two spoons for stirring, a cloth to wipe the thermometers, and a timer
a tray to stand the pan on, a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up boils the water, mixes the bath and sets the tumblers in it. The oil in this test is never put on a flame and never gets hotter than about 70 degrees. Work on a steady table with a tray under the pan. Glass thermometers break easily, so never stir with them, and lay them flat on a cloth. Wipe up any spilt oil at once, because it is slippery.

schedule.what: Guess. Measure the oil and the water. Make the bath. Read both every 3 minutes for 12 minutes. Draw the graph and say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw two lines on one graph, one for the oil and one for the water, with time along the bottom. Write how many degrees each one rose in 12 minutes.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you put a tumbler of oil and a tumbler of water in the same hot bath. You find out which warms up more, and by how much.

setup.art: Two identical steel tumblers on a table, one with 100 millilitres of golden oil and one with 100 millilitres of water, each with a thermometer reading about the same.
setup.caption: 1. Put oil in one tumbler and water in the other. Both start at room temperature.

setup.art: A grown-up pouring hot water from a kettle into a wide pan on a tray, with a thermometer checking the bath.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up makes a hot bath about 70 degrees.

setup.art: The two tumblers standing side by side in the pan of hot water, with thermometers in them, a timer, and a notebook.
setup.caption: 3. Stand both tumblers in the bath. Read and stir every 3 minutes.

flow.do: Show your child the two tumblers, the oil, the water and the thermometers. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write both down at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will put one tumbler of oil and one of water in the same hot bath. After 12 minutes, which will have warmed up more? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Oil and water in the same hot bath. Which warms more? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will warm up more?
good: Oil is thinner, so heat gets in quickly.
Water soaks up heat.
They will warm the same, because the bath is the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children expect water to warm faster, because water feels hot so quickly. Others expect no difference. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Oil and Water test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Measure 100 millilitres of oil into one tumbler and 100 millilitres of water into the other. Stand a thermometer in each. Wait until both lines stop. Write the two starting numbers.
flow.say: Here are 100 millilitres of oil and 100 millilitres of water. Both have stood in the room for a while. Let's see if they start at the same temperature.
flow.kid: Pour 100 millilitres of oil in one tumbler. Pour 100 millilitres of water in the other. Read both.
flow.parent: Both tumblers should read within a degree of each other, near the room temperature. If the oil came from a cold shelf, wait until it matches. Equal volumes of oil and water do not have exactly equal masses, because oil is a little lighter. That does not change the result, which is much bigger.

check.q: Why must both tumblers start at the same temperature?
options: So that only the liquid changes, and the difference comes from the liquid
So the oil does not catch fire
So the bath is not too hot
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If one tumbler started warmer, you could not tell whether the liquid or the start made the difference.

flow.context: In this step, you pour the oil and water and write down their starting temperatures.

flow.do: A grown-up mixes boiled water and tap water in a wide pan, to about 70 degrees. The bath should be about 3 centimetres deep. Check it with a thermometer. Stand both tumblers in the pan side by side, and start the timer.
flow.say: I am making the bath now, because it is hot. The water in the pan should come up to about the same height as the liquid inside each tumbler. Keep your hands away from the pan.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes the hot bath. Do not touch it. Watch both tumblers.
flow.parent: Aim for a bath of 65 to 70 degrees. A wide pan holds a lot of water, so it cools slowly. If a tumbler floats or tips, pour a little water out of the pan. Never put the oil on a flame in this test.
flow.context: In this step, a grown-up makes the hot bath and the tumblers go in.

flow.do: Every 3 minutes, for 12 minutes, stir each tumbler gently with its own spoon. Read the oil, then the water. Wipe the thermometers after each reading. Write both numbers. Read the bath at 6 and 12 minutes.
flow.say: Stir gently, then read the oil, then the water. Write both numbers. What do you notice about the two numbers as time goes on?
flow.kid: Stir. Read the oil. Read the water. Write both numbers. Again in 3 minutes.
flow.parent: A typical result in a 29 degree room, with a bath starting at 70: the oil reads 29, 41, 50, 56, 60. The water reads 29, 35, 40, 44, 47. The oil warms by about 31 degrees and the water by about 18, which is not quite twice as much but near it. Your numbers will differ. The bath cools by a few degrees. A thermometer in oil may need an extra wipe.

check.q: Why do we stir each liquid gently before every reading?
options: So the whole liquid is at one temperature, and the reading is right
To make the liquid hotter
To let the heat out
check.why: Heat enters through the sides of the tumbler, so the liquid near the sides is warmer. Stirring mixes it, so the thermometer shows the temperature of the whole liquid.

flow.context: In this step, you stir and read both tumblers every 3 minutes for 12 minutes.

flow.do: Draw a line graph with two lines. Then ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw two lines on one graph. Then say what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: oil warms about twice as fast as water in the same bath. What I saw: the oil rose from 29 to 60, and the water from 29 to 47. Why: water needs about twice as much heat as oil for each degree, so the same heat warms the oil by more degrees.

check.q: In the same bath the oil warmed by about 30 degrees and the water by about 15. About how much more heat does water need for each degree?
options: About twice as much
About 15 times as much
The same, because the bath was the same
check.why: If the same heat warms the oil by twice as many degrees, then each degree of water needs about twice as much heat as each degree of oil. Picking the same heat is a common idea. The bath is the same, but the liquids answer it differently.

flow.context: In this step, you draw the graph and explain what happened, using what you think, what you saw, and why.

experiments.title: The Katori and the Bowl: which melts more ice?
experiments.question: A small katori holds hot water at 60 degrees. A big bowl holds warmer-than-room water at 40 degrees. If you put the same amount of ice in each, which melts more ice?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which will melt more ice, the hotter katori or the cooler bowl? Or will they melt the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Take the ice cubes from the same tray, and put the same number in each container at the same time. Stir both gently in the same way. Count the cubes left at the same times. Only the amount and the temperature of the water change, so the difference comes from them.

materials.item: a small steel katori that holds about 150 millilitres
a bowl that holds about 2 litres, and a measuring jug that holds 1 litre
12 ice cubes from the same tray, and a plate to stand them on. If they are very small, use 16 and put 8 in each.
hot water: half boiled and half tap water, mixed by a grown-up to about 60 degrees
a laboratory thermometer, or a digital probe
two spoons, a cloth, a timer, a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up boils the water, mixes it and pours it. The child does not touch the hot water. Wipe up any spills, because wet floors are slippery. Glass thermometers break easily, so never stir with them.

schedule.what: Guess. Make the hot katori and the warm bowl. Add the ice. Count the cubes left at 5 and 10 minutes.

experiments.record: Write the temperature of each container at the start and at the end. Write how many cubes were left at 5 and 10 minutes. Draw each container with the cubes left.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you add the same ice to a small katori of hot water and to a big bowl of warmer-than-room water, and find which one melts more.

setup.art: A small steel katori of hot water with a thermometer reading 60, beside a big bowl of water with a thermometer reading 40.
setup.caption: 1. Make the katori hot (60 degrees) and the bowl warm (40 degrees).

setup.art: A child's hands dropping six ice cubes into the katori and six into the bowl at the same time, with a timer.
setup.caption: 2. Add six ice cubes to each at the same moment.

setup.art: The katori with a few ice cubes still floating, and the bowl with no ice, and a notebook with a table.
setup.caption: 3. Stir gently. Count the cubes left at 5 and 10 minutes.

flow.do: Show your child the katori, the bowl and the ice. Explain that the katori will hold hotter water and the bowl will hold cooler water. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write both down.
flow.say: A small katori will hold hot water. A big bowl will hold warm water, but cooler than the katori. We will drop the same ice in both. Which will melt more? Why?
flow.kid: A small katori of very hot water. A big bowl of warm water. Which melts more ice? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will melt more ice?
good: The hotter water is stronger.
The bowl has more water, so more heat.
They will melt the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children say the hotter katori, because hotter seems stronger. That is the idea this test checks.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Katori and the Bowl test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up mixes half boiled and half tap water to about 60 degrees. Pour 100 millilitres into the katori. Fill the jug with 600 millilitres of tap water, add 400 millilitres of the hot mix, and pour it into the bowl. Read both temperatures and write them down.
flow.say: I am mixing the hot water now. The katori gets 100 millilitres at about 60 degrees. The bowl gets a whole litre, at about 40 degrees. Let's read both.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes the hot katori and the warm bowl. Read both. Write them down.
flow.parent: The katori should read about 60 and the bowl about 40. The bowl is cooler than the katori, but it holds ten times as much water. If your bowl reads 35 to 45, that is fine.
flow.context: In this step, a grown-up makes the hot katori and the warm bowl, and you read their temperatures.

flow.do: Take 12 ice cubes from the same tray. Let them stand on a plate for 2 minutes, so the surface starts to melt. Then put 6 in the katori and 6 in the bowl at the same moment. Start the timer.
flow.say: Six cubes in each, at the same moment. Why do we use the same number of cubes, from the same tray?
flow.kid: Put six ice cubes in each. Start the timer.
flow.parent: Standing the cubes for 2 minutes lets them reach about 0 degrees, rather than the freezer's minus 18. If the cubes are tiny and all melt in both containers, repeat with 12 cubes in each.

check.q: Why do we use the same number of ice cubes, from the same tray, in both?
options: So the only differences are the amount and the temperature of the water
So the katori does not overflow
So the ice is bigger
check.why: If one container got more ice, you could not tell whether the water or the ice made the difference. A fair test changes one thing at a time.

flow.context: In this step, you add the same ice to both containers.

flow.do: Stir both gently with a spoon. At 5 minutes and at 10 minutes, count the ice cubes still floating, big or small, and write the numbers. At 10 minutes, read both temperatures.
flow.say: Stir gently. How many cubes are left now? How many are left in the bowl? What is happening to each temperature?
flow.kid: Stir. Count the cubes left. Read the temperatures. Write them down.
flow.parent: A typical result: after 10 minutes the katori still has 1 or 2 small pieces, and reads about 0 to 2 degrees. The bowl has no ice, and reads about 25 degrees. The katori has too little heat to melt all its ice, even though it started hotter. If the katori melts all the ice too, add 4 more cubes to each and repeat.

check.q: The bowl started cooler than the katori, but melted more ice. Why?
options: The bowl held far more water, so it held far more heat to give
Cooler water melts ice better
The bowl is made of better metal
check.why: Melting ice needs heat, and the bowl has about ten times as much water, so it has far more heat to give. Picking cooler water makes sense if you did not expect the result. But temperature only tells how hot, not how much heat.

flow.context: In this step, you count the ice left and read the temperatures.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: how much heat a thing can give depends on how much of it there is, as well as on its temperature. What I saw: the katori at 60 melted only part of its ice, but the bowl at 40 melted all of its ice. Why: the bowl had ten times as much water, so ten times as much heat to give away for each degree it cooled.

check.q: If the bowl held only 100 millilitres of water at 40 degrees, like the katori, which would melt more ice?
options: The katori at 60 degrees, because it is hotter and holds the same amount
The bowl, because it is cooler
They would melt the same
check.why: With equal amounts, the hotter water holds more heat, so it melts more ice. In the test, the bowl won only because it held ten times as much water.

flow.context: In this step, you explain what happened, using what you think, what you saw, and why.

experiments.title: Stuck at Zero: where does the heat go while ice melts?
experiments.question: If you stand a tumbler of crushed ice in a bath of warm water, how does the thermometer in the ice change as the ice melts?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Heat will flow into the ice from the warm bath. Will the thermometer rise steadily, stay still for a while, or jump? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Read the thermometer at the same times, every 2 minutes. Stir the ice gently with a spoon, never with the thermometer. Keep the same bath for the whole test. This test has one change, which is time, so we watch how the reading changes as heat keeps going in.

materials.item: a laboratory thermometer that reads from about minus 10 to 110 °C, or a digital probe
a steel tumbler of about 250 millilitres, and a cup for measuring 50 millilitres of water
10 ice cubes, a clean cloth and a rolling pin, for cracking the ice
a basin with about 2 litres of warm tap water, as warm as a pleasant bath, about 35 to 40 degrees
a spoon for stirring, a timer, a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up cracks the ice and mixes the warm water. Keep the bath no hotter than a pleasant bath. Wipe up any water, because wet floors are slippery. Glass thermometers break easily, so never stir with them and lay them flat on a cloth.

schedule.what: Guess. Crack the ice. Stand the tumbler in the bath. Read it every 2 minutes for 24 minutes. Draw the graph and say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a line graph with time along the bottom and temperature up the side. Circle the flat part, and write when the last ice melted.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you watch a thermometer in melting ice. The warm bath keeps giving heat, and you see what happens to the temperature.

setup.art: A rolling pin cracking ice cubes wrapped in a cloth on a chopping board, with a child watching.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cracks ten ice cubes in a cloth.

setup.art: A steel tumbler of cracked ice and a little cold water, with a thermometer standing in it, and a spoon.
setup.caption: 2. Put the ice in the tumbler with a little cold water. Stand the thermometer in it.

setup.art: The tumbler standing in a basin of warm water, a timer beside it, and a notebook with a graph being drawn.
setup.caption: 3. Stand the tumbler in the warm bath. Read it every 2 minutes.

flow.do: Show your child the ice, the thermometer and the bath. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write both down.
flow.say: We will stand a tumbler of ice in warm water. Heat will keep flowing into the ice. What will the thermometer do? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Warm water heats the ice. What will the thermometer do? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the thermometer will do that?
good: Heat is going in, so it will rise.
It will stay at zero until the ice is gone.
It will jump up quickly.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children expect a steady rise. The flat part is the surprise of this test.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Stuck at Zero test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up wraps 10 ice cubes in a cloth and cracks them with a rolling pin. Put the pieces in the steel tumbler, with 50 millilitres of cold tap water. Stir with a spoon. Stand the thermometer in it and wait until the reading stops. Write the start.
flow.say: I am cracking the ice into small pieces, so it can melt faster. The thermometer should read about zero. Is that what it reads?
flow.kid: A grown-up cracks the ice. Put it in the tumbler with a little cold water. Read the thermometer.
flow.parent: Ice that has just come out of a freezer can read 1 to 3 degrees below zero at first. After a minute of stirring it should settle at about 0. The thermometer is not exact, so a reading from minus 1 to 1 counts as zero.
flow.context: In this step, you cracked ice into a tumbler and read the starting temperature.

flow.do: A grown-up fills the basin with 2 litres of warm tap water, about as warm as a pleasant bath. Stand the tumbler in the basin, so the water outside comes up the tumbler's side by about 4 centimetres. Start the timer.
flow.say: Here is the warm bath. Heat can only flow one way, from the warm bath into the cold ice. Let's start the timer.
flow.kid: A grown-up fills the basin with warm water. Stand the tumbler in it. Start the timer.
flow.parent: If the bath is cooler than about 30 degrees, the ice melts slowly and the test takes much longer. Ask a grown-up to add a little warm water. The bath is large so that it stays warm all through the test.
flow.context: In this step, you stand the tumbler of ice in a basin of warm water and start the timer.

flow.do: Every 2 minutes, stir the ice gently with the spoon. Read the thermometer. Write the number and whether there is ice left. Keep going until all the ice is gone and the reading has risen at least 5 degrees.
flow.say: Stir gently, then read. What number is it now? Is there ice left? What is the thermometer doing?
flow.kid: Stir. Read. Write the number. Is there ice left? Again in 2 minutes.
flow.parent: A typical result: 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 5, 10, 15, 20, 24 at the 2-minute marks. The reading stays at zero for 10 to 14 minutes, while there is ice, and then climbs fast once the last ice has gone. Your times will differ, but the flat part should appear. If the reading never stays flat, the bath may be too hot or the ice too small. Try again with fewer, bigger pieces.

check.q: For ten minutes the thermometer stayed at 0, though the bath kept giving heat. Where was the heat going?
options: Into melting the ice, by pulling its particles apart
It was lost into the air
It was going into the thermometer
check.why: The heat was being used up in turning ice into water. This hidden heat is called latent heat. Picking the air is a good thought, but the bath was keeping the water warmer than the air.

flow.context: In this step, you read the thermometer every 2 minutes as the ice melts.

flow.do: Draw a line graph. Circle the flat part. Then ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw the graph. Circle the flat part. Say what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: while ice melts, heat goes in but the temperature stays at zero. What I saw: the reading stayed at 0 for about 12 minutes, and then rose quickly after the last ice melted. Why: the heat was used to melt the ice, and only when the ice was gone could the heat make the water warmer.

check.q: At the moment the last ice melted, what did the thermometer start to do?
options: Rise quickly, because the heat now went into warming the water
Stay at zero for ever
Fall below zero
check.why: Once there is no ice left to melt, all the heat goes into making the water particles move faster, so the temperature climbs.

flow.context: In this step, you draw the graph and explain what happened, using what you think, what you saw, and why.

activities.title: The Balloon on the Bottle: does warm air take up more room?

materials.item: an empty, dry plastic bottle of 1 litre, with thin smooth sides
a small round balloon, stretched a few times by blowing it up and letting the air out
a soft string or a tape measure, and a ruler
two basins: one for hot water, about as hot as a cup of tea for drinking, and one for ice water
a thermometer, a timer, a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up pours the hot water. It must not be boiling, because a thin plastic bottle goes soft in very hot water. Hold the bottle by its neck. Do not blow up the balloon while it sits on the bottle.

schedule.what: Guess. Fit the balloon. Stand the bottle in hot water, then in ice water. Measure the balloon each time.

activities.record: Draw the bottle and balloon three times: at the start, in hot water and in ice water. Write the measurement round the balloon under each drawing.
activities.context: In this activity, you fit a balloon on a bottle and stand the bottle in hot water and then in ice water. You find out what happens to the air inside.

setup.art: A flat balloon stretched over the mouth of an empty plastic bottle, with a child wrapping a string round the widest part of the balloon.
setup.caption: 1. Fit the balloon on the bottle. Measure round the widest part.

setup.art: The bottle standing in a basin of hot water, with the balloon half blown up.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up pours hot water. Stand the bottle in it and watch the balloon.

setup.art: The same bottle standing in a basin of ice water, with the balloon sagging and flat again.
setup.caption: 3. Move the bottle into ice water. Watch the balloon again.

flow.do: Show your child the bottle, the balloon and the two basins. Ask for a guess about the hot water and the ice water, with a reason. Write both down.
flow.say: The balloon sits on the bottle. We stand the bottle in hot water. What will the balloon do? Then we stand it in ice water. What will it do? Why?
flow.kid: A balloon on a bottle. Hot water. Ice water. What happens to the balloon? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the balloon will do that?
good: The hot water goes in the bottle and pushes the balloon.
The air inside gets bigger when warm.
Nothing will happen.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children think the hot water or steam gets in. The bottle stays closed, so only the air already inside is involved.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Balloon on the Bottle. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Fit the balloon over the mouth of the empty bottle. Wrap a string round the widest part of the balloon, and measure the string with a ruler. Write it down as the start.
flow.say: The bottle looks empty, but it is full of air. The balloon seals the air inside. Measure round the balloon. What does the string measure?
flow.kid: Fit the balloon on the bottle. Measure round it. Write the number.
flow.parent: The balloon will be flat, so the string measure is small, perhaps 4 to 6 centimetres. The balloon must fit tightly. If you can hear air hissing out, press the neck of the balloon down or use another balloon.
flow.context: In this step, you fit the balloon on the bottle and measure it.

flow.do: A grown-up pours hot water, about 5 centimetres deep, into a basin. Stand the bottle in the water and hold it by its neck. Watch the balloon for 3 to 4 minutes. Then measure round the balloon again.
flow.say: Watch the balloon. What is it doing? Is the bottle leaking? Where is the air coming from?
flow.kid: A grown-up pours the hot water. Stand the bottle in it. Watch the balloon.
flow.parent: Expect the balloon to swell slowly to the size of a lime or even an orange, and the string measure to climb to 15 to 25 centimetres. The balloon has to stretch before it starts, so the first minute can look slow. If nothing happens, the balloon may be too stiff or leaking.

check.q: The balloon swelled up in the hot water, but the bottle was closed. Where did the extra air come from?
options: Nowhere. The air already inside took up more room
Steam came in through the bottle
The hot water turned into air
check.why: The bottle and balloon were sealed. No air could come in. The same air took up more room when it was warm, so it pushed the balloon out. This is expansion.

flow.context: In this step, you stand the bottle in hot water and watch the balloon swell.

flow.do: Lift the bottle out of the hot water and stand it in a basin of ice water for 4 minutes. Measure round the balloon again.
flow.say: Now we cool the air. What will happen to the balloon? Why do you think so? Measure round it again.
flow.kid: Stand the bottle in ice water. Watch the balloon. Measure it again.
flow.parent: The balloon sags and shrinks back, sometimes even drawing slightly into the bottle. The air has cooled and taken up less room. This is contraction.
flow.context: In this step, you cool the air in the bottle and watch the balloon shrink.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: warm air takes up more room than cool air. What I saw: the balloon swelled in hot water and shrank in ice water. Why: heat made the air particles move faster and push further apart.
flow.think: Air grows by about 1 part in 270 for each degree. Why does a bicycle tyre feel harder after a ride on a hot road?
flow.context: In this step, you explain what happened, using what you think, what you saw, and why.

activities.title: Heat from Movement: hands, a paper clip and a rubber band

materials.item: a large metal paper clip, straightened out a little so it bends easily
a thick rubber band
your own hands, and a table top or a cloth
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up watches the paper clip test. Bend the clip no more than 15 times, because it can snap, and a broken clip can be sharp and hot. Bend it away from your face. Touch the bend only lightly and briefly to your upper lip or wrist. If it feels too hot, stop.

schedule.what: Make heat three ways and feel the warmth. Think about where the heat came from.

activities.record: Make a table with three rows: hands, paper clip and rubber band. For each, write how many seconds or bends you used, and whether it felt a little warm, warm or very warm.
activities.context: In this activity, you make heat by rubbing, bending and stretching, with no flame at all. You find out where the heat comes from.

setup.art: A child rubbing their palms together fast, with small curved lines for warmth between the hands.
setup.caption: 1. Rub your hands together hard for 20 seconds.

setup.art: A child bending a paper clip back and forth many times, held away from the face, with a grown-up watching.
setup.caption: 2. Bend the clip back and forth 15 times, quickly.

setup.art: A child stretching a thick rubber band quickly, then pressing it lightly to the upper lip.
setup.caption: 3. Stretch the rubber band quickly 10 times, then press it to your lip.

flow.do: Ask your child to rub both palms together hard for 20 seconds, then stop and press them to their cheeks. Ask where the warmth came from.
flow.say: Rub your hands together hard for 20 seconds. Then press them on your cheeks. How warm are they? Where did that warmth come from?
flow.kid: Rub your hands hard for 20 seconds. Press them to your cheeks. Are they warm?

ask.q: Where did the warmth come from?
good: From my moving hands.
From the rubbing.
From my body, because my hands were already warm.

flow.parent: Do not correct the answer. Some children say the warmth was hidden inside the hands. Ask: if I rub for an hour, will they keep getting warmer? A hidden store of heat would run out.
flow.context: This is the first step of Heat from Movement. You make heat with your hands.

flow.do: A grown-up watches. Bend the paper clip back and forth 15 times, quickly, away from the face. Then touch the bend lightly to the upper lip or the wrist. Compare it with a part of the clip that was not bent.
flow.say: Bend the clip back and forth, 15 times, fast. Then touch the bend to your lip, only lightly. Now touch a part you did not bend. What do you notice?
flow.kid: A grown-up watches. Bend the clip 15 times. Touch the bend lightly to your lip.
flow.parent: The bend should feel clearly warmer than the straight part. If it feels only slightly warm, bend it 5 more times, but stop before 20. Never bend until it snaps.

check.q: The bend of the paper clip felt warmer than the straight part. Why?
options: The movement of bending turned into heat in the metal
The clip was warm from your hand
Bending a clip lets in heat from the air
check.why: Bending pushes and drags the metal's particles past each other, and the movement energy of your hand turns into jiggling of particles. That is heat. The straight part was not bent, so it did not get this extra heat.

flow.context: In this step, you bend a paper clip and feel the heat in the bend.

flow.do: Stretch the thick rubber band quickly 10 times. Hold it stretched against your upper lip for a moment, then let it go slack and press it to your lip again.
flow.say: Stretch the rubber band fast, ten times. Press it to your lip while it is stretched. Then let it go slack. What do you feel?
flow.kid: Stretch the band ten times. Press it to your lip. Then let it relax. Press again.
flow.parent: A stretched band feels slightly warmer. When it relaxes, it feels slightly cooler. The effect is small but real, and a thick band shows it best. Rubber is unusual: stretching it makes it warm, and letting it relax cools it.
flow.context: In this step, you stretch a rubber band and feel it warm up and cool down.

flow.do: Talk about the three tests together. Ask where the heat came from each time. Then tell the story of James Joule, who measured how much heat the same movement always makes.
flow.say: In every test, you moved something, and it got warm. James Joule measured this about 180 years ago. He found that the same amount of movement always makes the same amount of heat. What does that tell you?
flow.kid: Movement can turn into heat. Where did the heat come from each time?
flow.think: If rubbing could make heat without end, could heat be a fluid stored inside things? What else could heat be?
flow.context: In this step, you think about what the three tests have in common.

activities.title: Wet and Dry: does water on a thermometer cool it?

materials.item: two thermometers, or one thermometer used twice
a strip of thin cotton cloth, about 5 centimetres wide, cut in two
two rubber bands, a bowl of tap water, a stiff card to use as a fan
a bottle of water and a second bottle of the same size, for the extra test
a timer, a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Hold glass thermometers by the top and lay them flat on a cloth when you are not holding them. Keep the thermometers out of direct sun, so that you measure the air and not the sunshine.

schedule.what: Guess. Read the dry air. Wrap one thermometer in wet cloth and the other in dry cloth. Fan both and read them.

activities.record: Make a table with the dry-cloth reading, the wet-cloth reading and the difference, at the start and after 3 minutes of fanning. Write what the air felt like that day: dry or humid.
activities.context: In this activity, you wrap a wet cloth around one thermometer and a dry cloth around another, and find out which reads lower and why.

setup.art: Two thermometers side by side on a table, one with a wet cotton cloth tied round its bulb and one with a dry cloth tied round its bulb.
setup.caption: 1. Tie wet cloth on one thermometer and dry cloth on the other.

setup.art: A child fanning both thermometers with a stiff card, with a timer beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Fan both for 3 minutes.

setup.art: The two thermometers with the wet one clearly lower than the dry one, and a notebook with a table.
setup.caption: 3. Read both and write the difference.

flow.do: Ask your child to feel a bit of wet cloth on the back of the hand, then blow on it. Ask for a guess about the thermometers, with a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: Put a wet cloth on your hand and blow on it. It feels cool. Now, a thermometer wrapped in wet cloth, and one wrapped in dry cloth. Which reads lower? Why?
flow.kid: Wet cloth on a thermometer. Dry cloth on another. Which reads lower? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will read lower?
good: The wet one is cold from the water.
The water takes the heat away as it dries.
They will read the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Some will say the water is cold. The tap water is at the same temperature as the room.
flow.context: This is the first step of Wet and Dry. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Read both thermometers in the air in a shady spot, and write the starting numbers. They should match. Dip one strip of cloth in tap water and squeeze it so it does not drip. Tie it round one bulb with a rubber band. Tie a dry strip round the other bulb.
flow.say: First we check that both thermometers agree in the air. Then one gets a wet jacket and one gets a dry jacket. Why does the other one get a dry jacket?
flow.kid: Read both thermometers. Tie a wet cloth round one. Tie a dry cloth round the other.
flow.parent: Use the same kind of cloth for both. Keep the thermometers away from direct sun.

check.q: Why do we put a dry cloth on the second thermometer, rather than leave it bare?
options: So the only difference is the water, not the cloth
To keep it warm
So it does not break
check.why: The cloth might change the reading by itself, for example by blocking air. If both thermometers wear a cloth, the water is the only thing that differs.

flow.context: In this step, you read both thermometers and put the wet and dry cloths on.

flow.do: Fan both thermometers with the stiff card for 3 minutes, from the same distance. Read both. Write the numbers and the difference. Try a second time if you like, wetting the cloth again.
flow.say: Fan them both for three minutes, the same way. Read both. Which is lower? By how many degrees?
flow.kid: Fan both for three minutes. Read both. Write the difference.
flow.parent: On a dry day, the wet thermometer often reads 3 to 6 degrees lower. In a very humid time, such as the Chennai or Mumbai monsoon, it may read only 1 or 2 degrees lower, because the air is already full of water and cannot take more. Either result is real, and tells you about the air.

check.q: Why did the thermometer with the wet cloth read lower?
options: As the water evaporated, it took heat from the bulb
The water was colder than the room
The wet cloth kept the heat out
check.why: Evaporating water takes heat from what it leaves, which cooled the bulb. The tap water began at the room's temperature. The dry cloth stayed at the air's temperature.

flow.context: In this step, you fan the thermometers and read them.

flow.do: Optional extra. Wrap one of the two same-sized water bottles in a wet cloth and leave it in a breeze for 20 minutes. Leave the other bottle bare. Then read the water in both.
flow.say: Here is the clay matka trick, with a bottle. One bottle wears a wet cloth. One is bare. After twenty minutes, which water is cooler? Why?
flow.kid: One wet-wrapped bottle. One bare bottle. After twenty minutes, which is cooler?
flow.parent: The wet-wrapped bottle is usually 1 to 3 degrees cooler, if there is a breeze and the air is not very humid. This is how a clay matka keeps water cool.
flow.think: In which month would the wet cloth cool the bottle more in your town, a dry month or a rainy month? Why?
flow.context: In this step, you test the matka trick with a wet cloth around a bottle.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: evaporating water cools what it leaves. What I saw: the wet thermometer read lower than the dry one. Why: the fastest water particles leave and carry heat away.
flow.context: In this step, you explain what happened, using what you think, what you saw, and why.

activities.title: How much heat is in a groundnut?

materials.item: one raw unsalted groundnut kernel, or a small piece of dry coconut (copra) if anyone at home has a nut allergy
a bamboo skewer or a long pin, and a lump of atta dough to hold it upright
a small thin steel katori, and 100 millilitres of tap water measured with a cup
a pair of tongs or a folded cloth, a long match or lighter, a steel plate, and a bowl of water for safety
a thermometer, a spoon, a notebook and a pencil
a kitchen scale that reads in grams, if you have one

activities.safety: A grown-up does every step with fire. Tie back long hair and roll up sleeves. Work on a steel plate on a table, with a bowl of water close by, and open a window. Never do this if anyone at home has a nut allergy, because the smoke carries oil from the nut. Use a piece of dry coconut instead. Never leave the flame, and let everything cool before you touch it.

schedule.what: Guess. Set up the groundnut and the katori. A grown-up burns the nut under the water. Work out the heat.

activities.record: Write the water's starting temperature, its highest temperature, and the rise. Multiply the rise by 100 to get the calories the water caught. Compare it with the heat in a groundnut.
activities.context: In this activity, a grown-up burns a groundnut under a katori of water. You measure how much heat the food gives, in calories.

setup.art: A groundnut stuck on the end of a skewer standing in a lump of dough on a steel plate, with a bowl of water close by.
setup.caption: 1. Stick the groundnut on the skewer and stand it in dough.

setup.art: A small steel katori with 100 millilitres of water and a thermometer, held in tongs above the groundnut.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the katori of water 3 centimetres above the nut.

setup.art: A grown-up lighting the groundnut with a long match while the katori hovers above, and a child reading the thermometer.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up lights the nut. The flame heats the water.

flow.do: Explain that food holds heat, which our bodies release slowly. Ask your child to guess how many degrees 100 millilitres of water will rise when one groundnut burns under it. Write the guess.
flow.say: A groundnut is food, and food holds heat. We will burn one under a katori of water. How many degrees do you think the water will rise? One? Ten? Fifty? Why?
flow.kid: Burn a groundnut under water. How many degrees will the water rise? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think so many degrees, or so few?
good: The nut is small, so just a few degrees.
A flame is hot, so many degrees.
The nut has lots of oil, so lots of heat.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A single groundnut kernel holds about 3 kilocalories, which is 3,000 calories. In theory, that could warm 100 grams of water by 30 degrees. In this test, most of the heat escapes, so the real rise is smaller.
flow.context: This is the first step of How much heat is in a groundnut. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up sets up everything. Push the skewer into the groundnut, and stand the skewer in the dough on the steel plate. Pour 100 millilitres of water into the katori and stand the thermometer in it. Read the starting temperature and write it down.
flow.say: I am setting up the fire part, so you will not touch it. The katori hangs about 3 centimetres above the nut. First, we read the water. What does it say?
flow.kid: A grown-up sets up the groundnut and the katori. Read the water's temperature. Write it down.
flow.parent: If you have a kitchen scale, weigh the nut before, and the leftover charred nut after. The difference in grams shows how much burned. Do not stir with the thermometer while it is over the flame.
flow.context: In this step, a grown-up sets up the groundnut and the katori of water.

flow.do: A grown-up lights the nut with a long match. At once, hold the katori in tongs about 3 centimetres above the flame. Keep it there until the flame goes out. If the nut stops burning, relight it quickly. Then stir the water with a spoon and read the highest temperature.
flow.say: Watch the flame under the katori. It heats the water. When the flame dies, we stir the water and read the thermometer. Stand back from the fire.
flow.kid: A grown-up lights the nut. Watch the water. When the flame dies, read the thermometer.
flow.parent: A groundnut often burns for 30 seconds to a minute. If it will not catch fire, hold the match to it for a few seconds, or use dry coconut. Keep the katori steady and close. The water usually rises 5 to 15 degrees. Keep the pin's tip away from fingers. Put the burnt nut in the bowl of water.

check.q: Why is it safe to keep the katori close to the flame, rather than far above it?
options: More of the flame's heat goes into the water, and less is lost to the air
The flame burns longer
The water stays cooler
check.why: The closer the katori, the more heat reaches the water. But it cannot be so close that it smothers the flame. This also shows that a lot of the heat always escapes.

flow.context: In this step, a grown-up burns the nut under the water and you read the temperature.

flow.do: Work out the heat the water caught. Take the rise in degrees and multiply by 100, because there are 100 grams of water. For example, a rise of 8 degrees is 800 calories. Write your answer in calories.
flow.say: The water rose by some degrees. Each degree for 100 grams of water takes 100 calories. So how many calories did your water catch?
flow.kid: Rise in degrees times 100 is the calories. How many did your water catch?
flow.parent: For example, a rise of 8 degrees means 8 times 100, which is 800 calories. Check the sum together. If your child is unsure, use a ruler line as a number line and count in hundreds.
flow.context: In this step, you work out how many calories the water caught.

flow.do: Tell your child that a raw groundnut kernel holds roughly 3,000 to 6,000 calories, depending on its size. Compare it with the water's answer. Ask where the rest of the heat went.
flow.say: A real groundnut holds about three thousand calories or more. Your water caught fewer. Where do you think the rest of the heat went?
flow.kid: A groundnut holds about 3,000 calories. Your water caught fewer. Where did the rest go?

ask.q: Where did the rest of the heat go?
good: Into the air.
Into the katori and the thermometer.
Into the smoke and the hot gases.

flow.parent: Most of the heat warms the air around the flame, the katori and the smoke. A good home result catches a quarter to a third of the heat. This is why scientists in a proper laboratory put the flame inside a closed container. Good measuring includes saying how much you may have lost.
flow.think: Your body also gets about 5 kilocalories from each gram of groundnut. What does your body do with it?
flow.context: In this step, you compare your result with the real heat in a groundnut and think about where the rest went.

projects.title: Sand and Water in the Sun: two plates, two days

materials.item: two identical shallow steel plates or two identical plastic boxes with low sides
dry sand or dry fine soil, enough to fill one plate to a depth of 2 centimetres
tap water, enough to fill the other plate to the same depth of 2 centimetres
two thermometers, or one thermometer used twice at each time
a sunny balcony, window sill or terrace, and tape to hold the thermometers
a notebook with a table, and a pencil

projects.safety: Tie or tape the thermometers so they cannot fall from the balcony. Keep the plates where small children and birds cannot knock them. At the end of day 2, pour out the water so that mosquitoes cannot breed in it.

schedule.what: In the early morning, set up the plates in the sun. Read both at 8 in the morning, at noon, at 4 in the afternoon and at 9 at night.
Read both at 6 in the morning. Draw a graph with two lines and say what you think, what you saw and why.

projects.record: A table with five times and two columns, sand and water. Then a line graph with two lines, time along the bottom and temperature up the side.
projects.context: In this two-day project, you put a plate of sand and a plate of water in the sun and read their temperatures through a day and a night. You find which one warms faster, and which cools faster.

setup.art: Two identical steel plates on a sunny balcony ledge, one filled with 2 centimetres of dry sand and the other with 2 centimetres of water, each with a thermometer.
setup.caption: 1. Fill one plate with sand and one with water, to the same depth. Put them in the sun.

setup.art: A child reading the thermometer in the sand at noon, with shadows short and the sun bright.
setup.caption: 2. Read both at 8 in the morning, at noon, at 4 and at 9 at night.

setup.art: A notebook with a line graph of two lines, the sand line going high and low and the water line staying flatter.
setup.caption: 3. Read both at 6 the next morning. Draw the two lines.

flow.do: Show your child the plates, the sand, the water and the thermometers. Ask for guesses and reasons. Which plate will be hotter at noon? Which will be warmer at 6 the next morning? Write the guesses down.
flow.say: Two plates in the sun, one with sand and one with water. Which will be hotter at noon? Which will be warmer next morning at 6? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Sand and water in the sun. Which is hotter at noon? Which is warmer at night? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the sand will be hotter, or the water?
good: Sand is dark, so it takes in more sun.
Water needs a lot of heat to warm.
They will be the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children have walked on hot sand at a beach and say sand will win at noon. The night comparison is the surprise for most.
flow.context: This is the first step of Sand and Water in the Sun. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Early in the morning, fill one plate with 2 centimetres of sand. Fill the other with 2 centimetres of water. Stand them side by side in the sun. Push one thermometer into the sand so its bulb is just under the surface, and stand the other in the water. Read both at 8 and write the numbers.
flow.say: Let's fill the plates to the same depth. We put a thermometer in each one. Both are in the sun together. Read them. What do they say now?
flow.kid: Fill one plate with sand and one with water. Put a thermometer in each. Read both.
flow.parent: Both plates must sit in the same sunny spot. The bulbs should be just under the surface and not touching the plate. If you only have one thermometer, read the sand first, then the water, each time, as quickly as you can. Note that equal depth means the sand weighs more than the water.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the plates and read their starting temperatures.

flow.do: Read both thermometers at noon and at 4 in the afternoon. Write the numbers. Stir the water gently before reading. Do not move the plates.
flow.say: Time for the noon reading. Which plate is hotter? By how many degrees? Look at the 4 o'clock numbers later. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Read both at noon. Write the numbers. Again at four.
flow.parent: On a clear day, expect the sand to be 5 to 15 degrees hotter than the water at noon. On a cloudy or rainy day, the difference can be small. If the day is cloudy, wait for a sunnier day and start again.
flow.wait: Come back at noon and again at 4 in the afternoon.
flow.context: In this step, you read the plates at noon and at 4 in the afternoon.

flow.do: Read both thermometers at 9 at night, and again at 6 the next morning. Write the numbers.
flow.say: It is night now. The sun has gone. Which plate is warmer? Is it the same plate that was hotter at noon?
flow.kid: Read both at night. Read both again in the morning. Write the numbers.
flow.parent: This is the surprising part. The sand, which was hottest at noon, is often the coolest by morning. The water changes less, so it is often the warmer plate at 6 in the morning, though it was cooler at noon.

check.q: The sand was hotter at noon, but the water was warmer at 6 the next morning. Why?
options: Water needs more heat for each degree, so it warms slowly and also cools slowly
Water makes its own heat at night
The sun warmed the water at night
check.why: Sand needs little heat for each degree, so it warms fast in the sun and loses its heat fast at night. Water needs a lot, so it changes slowly both ways. Nothing makes heat at night.

flow.wait: Come back at 9 at night, and then at 6 the next morning.
flow.context: In this step, you read the plates at night and in the early morning.

flow.do: Draw a line graph with two lines, sand and water. Then ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened. Pour out the water.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened? Then we pour the water away so that mosquitoes cannot breed.
flow.kid: Draw your two lines. Say what I think, what I saw, and why. Then pour out the water.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: sand warms and cools faster than water. What I saw: the sand reached 44 degrees at noon but fell to 26 by morning, while the water went only from 28 to 35 and back to 29. Why: water needs more heat for each degree, so it changes temperature slowly.
flow.think: How does this explain why a town by the sea has a smaller difference between day and night than a town in the desert?
flow.context: In this step, you draw the graph and explain what happened, using what you think, what you saw, and why.

challenges.title: The Warm Night Box: keep a box warm with one litre of hot water
challenges.problem: You have one litre of hot water at about 60 degrees, any jars or bottles, and a shoebox with a lid. Keep the air inside the shut box as warm as possible for 20 minutes in a cool place, such as the fridge, without using electricity or a flame.
constraints: Use no more than one litre of hot water in total, at about 60 degrees at the start.
The box must be shut during the test. Only a thermometer, or its wire, may poke out.
No electricity and no flame inside the box.
Test every design for the same time, 20 minutes, in the same cool place.
materials: a shoebox with a lid, and a cold place for it, such as a fridge shelf or a cool shaded balcony
a probe thermometer with a wire, or a laboratory thermometer to read through a slit in the lid
up to one litre of hot water from a grown-up, in steel tumblers, plastic bottles or jars. Plastic bottles must not be filled with boiling water.
old towels, newspaper, cloth and cardboard to try as wrappings
a timer, a notebook and a pencil
general: Put all the hot water in one big jar in the middle of the box. The more water, the more heat it holds, and the longer it keeps the air warm.
Fill a few small bottles and spread them around the box, so heat reaches all the air.
Wrap the shut box in a towel or newspaper, so that less heat escapes through the walls.
creative: Use a steel vessel for part of the water. Steel passes heat to the air faster than plastic, so the box warms up quickly.
Pack crumpled newspaper around the water jars to hold the air still, and leave a gap round the thermometer.
Put the box inside a bigger box with a layer of cloth between them.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your design. Build it and test it for 20 minutes. Change one thing, such as the number of bottles or the wrapping, and test again. Which design kept the box warmest? Why do you think it did?
challenges.safety: A grown-up pours the hot water. Do not use boiling water in plastic bottles. Tighten lids before moving a bottle. Keep the box away from small children, and wipe up any spill.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about heat stores. You use water to keep a shut box warm in a cold place.

setup.art: A shoebox with the lid off, holding one big jar of hot water in the middle and a probe thermometer, on a kitchen table.
setup.caption: 1. Put the hot water in jars inside the box. Add the thermometer.

setup.art: The shut shoebox sitting on a fridge shelf with the thermometer wire coming out, and a timer on the door.
setup.caption: 2. Shut the box. Put it in a cold place for 20 minutes.

setup.art: A notebook comparing two designs with readings, and two boxes side by side, one wrapped in a towel.
setup.caption: 3. Read the thermometer. Try a second design and compare.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the constraints. Ask your child which design would keep the box warmest, and why.
flow.say: You have one litre of hot water and a shoebox. How would you keep the box warm for twenty minutes in the cold? Why would your idea work?
flow.kid: A shoebox, one litre of hot water, a cold place. How will you keep it warm?

ask.q: What would keep the box warmer for longer?
good: Lots of water, because water holds a lot of heat.
A wrapping, so the heat stays in.
Smaller bottles.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Warm Night Box challenge. You plan.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw two or three designs. For each, say where the water goes, what the box is wrapped in, and where the thermometer sits.
flow.say: Draw two or three different designs first. Where will the water go? What will go round the box? Where does the thermometer sit?
flow.kid: Draw two or three designs. Show the water, the wrapping and the thermometer.
flow.think: Which will keep the box warmer: one big jar of hot water, or four small bottles with the same total water? Why?
flow.context: In this step, you plan your designs on paper.

flow.do: Build the first design. A grown-up pours the hot water. Put the thermometer in, shut the box, and put it in the cold place. Read the thermometer at the start, at 10 minutes and at 20 minutes. Write the numbers.
flow.say: Build your first design. A grown-up pours the water. Read the thermometer at the start, at ten minutes and at twenty minutes. Write down the numbers so you have a score to beat.
flow.kid: Build your box. A grown-up pours the water. Read at the start, ten minutes and twenty minutes.
flow.parent: Read the start before you shut the lid. Open a fridge door only briefly at each reading, or use a probe with a wire so you can read from outside. A typical result: the box starts at 28 and reads 36 or 38 with a big jar of hot water after 20 minutes in the fridge. A box with no water cools straight to about 10 or 12.
flow.context: In this step, you build and test your first design.

flow.do: Change one thing, such as the number of bottles or the wrapping, and test the second design the same way. Write the numbers in the same table.
flow.say: Change one thing. Test it the same way for twenty minutes. Write the numbers in the same table. Which design kept more heat?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again. Write the numbers. Which is warmer?
flow.parent: Change only one thing at a time, so you know what made the difference. Use fresh hot water at the same temperature.
flow.context: In this step, you change one thing and test again.

flow.do: Compare the two designs. Ask why the winner kept the box warmer, and how water helped.
flow.say: Which design won? Why do you think it kept the box warmer? What did the water do?
flow.kid: Which design won? Why? What did the water do?

check.q: Why did the box with hot water stay warmer than an empty box?
options: The water had a lot of heat to give, and gave it back slowly
The water made new heat
The water stopped the cold getting in
check.why: Water holds a lot of heat for each degree, so as it cools it gives a lot of heat to the air in the box. It does not make heat, and cold is not a thing that gets in. Heat goes out of the box more slowly because the water keeps topping it up.

flow.context: In this step, you compare your designs and say why the winner worked.
