quiz.p: A thermometer reads 40 °C in a big bucket of water and 40 °C in a small cup of water. What is true?
opts: They are at the same temperature, but the bucket holds far more heat
The bucket holds the same heat, because the temperature is the same
The cup holds more heat, because it is smaller
quiz.why: A thermometer shows how hot something is, not how much heat it holds. The bucket has far more water, so it holds far more heat. Picking the second answer is the most common slip.

quiz.p: Which unit is printed on food packets to show the heat in the food?
opts: Kilocalories
Degrees Celsius
Newtons
quiz.why: A kilocalorie is 1,000 calories, and a calorie is a unit of heat. Degrees Celsius measure temperature, and newtons measure force.

quiz.p: Which of these needs the most heat to warm by one degree?
opts: 100 grams of water
100 grams of cooking oil
100 grams of steel
quiz.why: Water needs about 1 calorie for each gram and each degree. Oil needs about half of that, and steel about a tenth. So water takes the most.

quiz.p: A tumbler of oil and a tumbler of water start at room temperature and stand in the same hot bath. After 12 minutes, what do you expect?
opts: The oil is hotter than the water
The water is hotter than the oil
They are exactly the same temperature
quiz.why: Oil needs less heat for each degree, so the heat from the bath warms it by more degrees. Picking exactly the same is common, because the bath is the same. But the liquids answer the bath differently.

quiz.p: A child wants to find out which of two liquids warms faster. Which is the fairest test?
opts: The same amount of each, starting at the same temperature, in the same hot bath
A big tumbler of one and a small tumbler of the other, in different baths
The same liquid at two different temperatures
quiz.why: A fair test changes only the liquid. Everything else, the amount, the start and the bath, stays the same.

quiz.p: A katori of water at 60 °C and a big bowl of water at 40 °C each get the same ice. Which melts more ice?
opts: The big bowl, because it holds far more heat
The katori, because it is hotter
They melt the same amount
quiz.why: The bowl has about ten times as much water, so it has far more heat to give, even though it is cooler. Picking the katori is a very natural guess. The test shows that amount matters as well as temperature.

quiz.p: Ice is melting in a glass of water. What does a thermometer in the ice read while there is still ice?
opts: About 0 °C
A number that keeps rising
About 100 °C
quiz.why: The heat that goes in is used to melt the ice, so the temperature holds at 0 °C until the last ice is gone.

quiz.p: Water boils in an open pot at sea level. You turn the flame up high. What happens to the temperature of the water?
opts: It stays at about 100 °C, and the water boils away faster
It rises to 200 °C
It falls, because the flame is too big
quiz.why: The extra heat goes into turning more water to steam. The water cannot go much above 100 °C while it boils in an open pot.

quiz.p: A paper clip bent back and forth many times gets warm at the bend. Where does the heat come from?
opts: From the movement of bending, which turns into heat
From a store of heat inside the clip
From the cold air
quiz.why: The movement energy of your hand makes the metal's particles jiggle faster. That is heat. A store would run out, but bending can keep making heat.

quiz.p: A balloon on a closed bottle swells when the bottle stands in hot water. Why?
opts: The air inside warms up and takes up more room
Hot water gets into the bottle
The bottle makes more air
quiz.why: The bottle is sealed, so no air can come in. The same air takes up more room when it is warm.

opts: When sweat evaporates, it takes heat away from your skin
Sweat is always colder than your skin
Sweat blocks the Sun's heat
quiz.why: The fastest water particles leave the skin as sweat evaporates, and they take their energy with them. Sweat starts at body temperature.

quiz.p: Why does a sandy beach get hot at noon while the sea beside it stays cool?
opts: Sand needs much less heat than water for each degree, so it warms faster
The Sun shines harder on the sand
Sand makes its own heat
quiz.why: The Sun shines about equally on both. Sand needs little heat for each degree, and sunlight only warms its top layer. The sea needs a lot of heat for each degree and mixes the heat through a deep layer.

quiz.p: People once thought a thermometer showed how much heat a thing holds. Which result shows this idea is wrong?
opts: A bucket of water at 40 °C can melt more ice than a katori of water at 60 °C
A thermometer takes about a minute to settle
Ice floats on water
quiz.why: If a thermometer showed the amount of heat, the hotter katori would melt more ice. It does not. So temperature and the amount of heat are different things, as Joseph Black showed in the 1760s.

items.p: One calorie is the heat that warms 1 gram of ____ by 1 degree Celsius.
items.why: The calorie was defined using water, because water is easy to find and easy to measure. Water needs 1 calorie for each gram and each degree.

items.p: A small katori of water is at 70 °C. A big bucket of water is at 40 °C. Which statement is true?
opts: The katori is hotter, but the bucket can give away more heat
The katori is hotter, and it can also give away more heat
The bucket is hotter, because it is bigger
items.why: Temperature tells how hot a thing is, and the katori is hotter. But the bucket has far more water, so it holds far more heat to give. Picking the second answer mixes up hot with how much heat.

items.p: Two things at the same temperature always hold the same amount of heat.
items.why: False. A bucket and a katori of water can be at the same temperature, but the bucket holds far more heat because it has far more water.

items.p: Kavya heats 100 grams of oil and 100 grams of water on the same stove for the same time. What happens?
opts: The oil warms by more degrees
The water warms by more degrees
Both warm by the same number of degrees
items.why: Oil needs only about half as much heat as water for each degree. So the same heat warms the oil by about twice as many degrees. Picking the same number of degrees is common, because the heat is the same. But the two liquids answer it differently.

items.p: Sort these. In the same sun for the same time, does each one warm up slowly or quickly?
items: 1 kilogram of water in a steel vessel
items.a: see items
items.why: Water, coconut water and milk are mostly water, so they need a lot of heat for each degree and warm slowly. Sand, iron and brick need much less heat for each degree, so they warm quickly.

items.p: Match each thing to what happens to its temperature.
pairs: Stays at 0 °C while any ice is left
Water boiling in an open pot at sea level
Water in a kettle that is warming up
A cup of tea left on the table
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: While a solid melts or a liquid boils, heat goes into changing the state and the temperature holds still. In the other two cases, the heat changes the temperature.

items.p: Put these in order, from the one that needs the least heat to warm by one degree (same mass), to the one that needs the most.
items.why: Gold needs about 0.03 calories for each gram and each degree. Steel needs about 0.1, dry sand about 0.2, oil about 0.5 and water 1. Water needs the most.

items.p: A chapati has about 100 kilocalories. How many calories is that?
opts: 100,000 calories
100 calories
1,000 calories
items.why: A kilocalorie is 1,000 calories. 100 times 1,000 is 100,000 calories. Picking 100 means forgetting that the 'kilo' means a thousand.

items.p: Sweat cools you because sweat is colder than your skin.
items.why: False. Sweat starts at about body temperature. It cools you by evaporating, which takes heat from your skin.

items.p: While ice is melting in a glass, a thermometer in the ice stays at ____ degrees Celsius.
items.why: The heat that goes in is used to melt the ice, so the temperature stays at 0 until the last ice has melted.

items.p: A steel spoon in a hot pan gets hot much faster than a cup of water in the same pan. Explain why.
items.a: Steel needs only about a tenth as much heat as water for each gram and each degree, and a spoon has little steel. So a small amount of heat warms it by a lot. The cup holds far more water, and water needs a lot of heat for each degree, so it warms slowly.
items.why: A strong answer says that different materials need different amounts of heat for each degree, and that a small spoon has little material to warm.

items.p: You rub your hands together hard for 20 seconds, and they get warm. Where did the heat come from?
items.a: From the movement of rubbing. The movement energy of the hands turned into heat, by making the tiny particles in the skin jiggle faster. It did not come from a store of heat inside the hands.
items.why: A strong answer says that movement turned into heat, and that you can keep rubbing for as long as you like, so the heat is not a store that runs out.

items.p: Draw two thermometers. Put one in melting ice and one in water boiling in an open pot at sea level. Write what each one reads.
items.a: The first thermometer shows 0 °C, in a glass with ice floating in water. The second shows about 100 °C, in a pot with bubbles and steam.
items.why: A strong drawing shows 0 and 100, and remembers that both stay at these numbers while the ice melts and while the water boils.
items.art: A blank box with space to draw a glass of ice water and a pot of boiling water, with two blank thermometers.

items.p: Label this drawing of a balloon on a bottle standing in hot water: balloon, bottle, warm air, hot water.
items.a: The balloon is on top of the bottle and swollen. The bottle is the clear plastic body below the balloon. The warm air is the air inside the bottle and balloon. The hot water is in the basin round the bottle.
items.why: The air inside is sealed in, and when it warms it expands and fills the balloon. Nothing comes in from outside.
items.art: A bottle standing in a basin of hot water with a swollen balloon on top and four blank label lines.

items.p: Why do bridges and railway tracks have small gaps in them?
opts: Steel grows longer when it warms, and needs room to expand
Steel shrinks in the sun, so the gaps fill up
The gaps let rainwater run through
items.why: Most solids expand when they warm. A long steel bridge can grow several centimetres on a hot day, and the gaps give it room. Picking the second answer has it backwards.

items.p: On a very humid day, the air is already full of water. How does this change the way sweat cools you?
opts: Sweat evaporates slowly, so you feel hotter than on a dry day at the same temperature
Sweat evaporates faster, so you feel cooler
Sweat does not matter, only the air temperature does
items.why: Sweat cools you only as fast as it evaporates. In humid air it evaporates slowly, so less heat leaves, and you feel hotter. This is why Chennai in the rains feels so sticky.

items.p: Look at the chart from the Oil and Water test. Both tumblers stood in the same bath for 12 minutes. What does the taller bar for the oil tell you?
opts: Oil needs less heat than water to warm by one degree
Oil was hotter than water at the start
Oil is a better conductor of electricity
items.why: Both tumblers got heat from the same bath. The oil rose by more degrees, so each degree of oil took less heat than each degree of water. Picking the second answer forgets that both started at the same temperature.

chart.title: Oil and Water: rise in temperature after 12 minutes

items.p: In an open pot, if you turn the flame up, boiling water gets hotter than 100 °C at sea level.
items.why: False. Boiling water stays at about 100 °C. More heat only makes it boil away faster.

items.p: A kilocalorie is ____ calories.
items.why: Kilo means a thousand. The Calories on food packets are kilocalories.

items.p: Three of these cool by evaporation. Which one does not?
opts: Sweat drying on your skin
Wet clothes drying on a line
A steel tumbler of tea cooling with a lid on it
Water inside a clay matka
items.why: Tea with a lid on cannot evaporate much, so it cools mostly by passing heat to the air and the table. The others all lose heat as water evaporates.

items.p: Sort these. Is the heat going into making it warmer, or into changing its state with no change in temperature?
items: Tap water warming from 28 °C to 60 °C in a kettle
Ice melting in a glass of lassi, still at 0 °C
Water boiling away in an open pot at 100 °C
A steel spoon warming in a hot pan
items.a: see items
items.why: While a solid is melting or a liquid is boiling, the heat goes into changing state, and the temperature holds still. Otherwise heat raises the temperature.

items.p: Put these steps in order for a fair test of which of two liquids warms faster.
items: Compare how many degrees each one rose
Put both in the same hot bath
Measure the same amount of each liquid
Make sure both start at room temperature
a: Measure the same amount of each liquid
Make sure both start at room temperature
Put both in the same hot bath
Compare how many degrees each one rose
items.why: A fair test keeps the amount, the start and the bath the same, and changes only the liquid. Then you read and compare.

items.p: Revathi says: the water must have got less heat from the bath than the oil, because it warmed less. What is wrong with her idea?
opts: Both got heat from the same bath. Water needs more heat for each degree, so it rose by fewer degrees
Nothing is wrong, she is right
Water cannot take in heat from a bath
items.why: A smaller rise in temperature does not mean less heat went in. Water needs more heat for each degree, so the same heat gives a smaller rise.

items.p: A bucket of water at 30 °C and a cup of tea at 70 °C. If you drop the same amount of ice into each, which would melt more? Explain your thinking.
items.a: The bucket would melt more ice. It has far more water, so it holds far more heat to give. The cup of tea is hotter, but it has little water, so it runs out of heat quickly.
items.why: A strong answer separates how hot a thing is from how much heat it can give, and uses the amount of water.

items.p: 100 grams of water is warmed from 28 °C to 78 °C. About how many calories does it need?
opts: 5,000 calories
500 calories
50 calories
items.why: The rise is 50 degrees. 100 grams times 50 degrees times 1 calorie is 5,000 calories. Picking 500 means using 10 degrees instead of 50.

items.p: Match each thing to the best reason for it.
pairs: Water needs a lot of heat for each degree
Steel needs little heat for each degree
Melting ice takes in a lot of heat
A wet cloth cools a bottle
A bridge has gaps in it
Steel grows longer when it warms
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each of these comes from one idea in this unit. The first two are about specific heat. The third is hidden heat. The fourth is evaporation, and the last is expansion.

items.p: Why does steam at 100 °C burn your skin worse than water at 100 °C?
opts: When steam turns back to water it gives out a lot of hidden heat
Steam is hotter than water at the same temperature
Steam is heavier than water
items.why: Each gram of steam gives out about 540 calories when it turns back into water, as well as the heat that the water then gives as it cools. This is the hidden heat of boiling.

items.p: On a dry day, a wet thermometer read 4 degrees lower than a dry one. In the monsoon, it read only 1 degree lower. Explain the difference.
items.a: In the monsoon, the air is already almost full of water, so water evaporates from the wet cloth very slowly. Less evaporation takes away less heat, so the wet thermometer cools less.
items.why: A strong answer links evaporation speed to the amount of water already in the air.

items.p: In the Sand and Water project, the sand was hotter at noon but cooler than the water at 6 the next morning. Explain why.
items.a: Sand needs little heat for each degree, so it warms fast in the sun and also loses its heat fast at night. Water needs a lot of heat for each degree, so it warms slowly and cools slowly. By morning the water had kept more of its heat.
items.why: A strong answer uses the same idea for the warming and the cooling: how much heat each degree takes.

items.p: Three friends argue about hot and heat.

views.says: A hotter thing always has more heat, because hot just means a lot of heat.
A bucket of warm water has more heat than a cup of hot tea. So the amount matters as well as the temperature.
Heat and temperature are two words for the same thing.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Use something from this unit as evidence. Then say what another friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer usually agrees with Farhan: the bucket and katori test showed that a cooler bowl can melt more ice. It admits that Kavya has a point, since between two equal amounts of the same thing, the hotter one does hold more heat. It explains that heat and temperature are different, which Meenakshi's idea misses.
items.why: There is a real argument here. Scientists once agreed with Kavya and Meenakshi, until Joseph Black showed that temperature and the amount of heat are different. A strong answer uses evidence and is fair to the other friends.

items.p: Draw a graph of temperature against time for a lump of ice that is warmed steadily until it becomes warm water. Mark the flat part.
items.a: The line rises from below zero to 0, then stays flat while the ice melts, then rises again as the water warms.
items.why: A strong graph has a flat piece at 0, where the heat is melting the ice.
items.art: A blank graph with time along the bottom and temperature up the side, with a dotted line at 0.

items.p: A bigger flame under a pot of boiling water makes the water boil away faster.
items.why: True. The extra heat goes into turning water to steam, so the water boils away faster. The temperature of the water stays at about 100 °C.

items.p: A big steel pot of dal and a small bowl of dal are both at 80 °C. Which cools more slowly?
opts: The big pot, because it holds far more heat
The small bowl, because it is smaller
They cool at the same speed
items.why: The pot holds far more dal and so far more heat. It loses heat through its surface, but it has less surface for each spoonful of dal, so it stays hot longer.

items.p: A grown-up warms 250 grams of water from 30 °C to 50 °C. About how many calories does that take?
opts: 5,000 calories
500 calories
50,000 calories
items.why: The rise is 20 degrees. 250 grams times 20 degrees times 1 calorie is 5,000 calories. Picking 50,000 puts in a zero too many.

items.p: Radha heats 100 grams of oil and 100 grams of water with the same candle for the same time. The oil rises by 40 degrees. About how much does the water rise? Show your thinking.
items.a: About 20 degrees. Oil needs about half as much heat as water for each degree. So the same heat warms the water by about half as many degrees as the oil.
items.why: A strong answer uses the ratio of specific heats, one half, to turn 40 into 20.

items.p: 1 litre of water at 90 °C is mixed with 2 litres of water at 30 °C. About what temperature will the mix reach?
opts: About 50 °C
About 60 °C
About 40 °C
items.why: Multiply each amount by its temperature: 1 times 90 is 90, and 2 times 30 is 60. The total is 150. Divide by 3 litres to get 50. The mix is nearer the 30 because there is more of it.

items.p: A block of ice taken from a freezer at minus 10 °C first warms up to 0 °C, and only then begins to melt.
items.why: True. Heat first makes the ice warmer. Only when it reaches 0 °C does the heat go into melting it.

items.p: A drink with ice cubes in it stays cold for much longer than the same drink with the same amount of cold water. Explain why.
items.a: Melting ice takes in a lot of heat, 80 calories for each gram, and the ice stays at 0 °C while it melts. So the ice soaks up heat from the drink for a long time and keeps the drink cold.
items.why: A strong answer names the hidden heat of melting, and says that the ice stays at 0 degrees while it takes in heat.

items.p: Why does a wet cloth on your forehead make you feel cooler?
opts: As the water evaporates, it takes heat from your skin
The water is always colder than your skin
The cloth stops heat from the Sun
items.why: Evaporation takes about 540 calories from the skin for each gram of water that leaves. The water on the cloth starts near room temperature.

items.p: Melting 1 gram of ice takes about ____ calories.
items.why: It takes as much heat as it takes to warm 1 gram of water by 80 degrees. The temperature stays at 0 °C while this heat goes in.

items.p: A 100-gram steel ladle needs about 10 calories for each degree. 100 grams of water needs about 100. Each gets 300 calories. About how much does each warm up?
opts: Steel by about 30 degrees, water by about 3 degrees
Steel by about 3 degrees, water by about 30 degrees
Both by about 15 degrees
items.why: Steel: 300 divided by 10 is 30 degrees. Water: 300 divided by 100 is 3 degrees. The material that needs less heat for each degree warms by more.

items.p: In the Katori and the Bowl test, the katori held 100 grams of water at 60 °C. If it cooled all the way to 0 °C, about how many grams of ice could it melt? Hint: it takes 80 calories to melt 1 gram.
items.a: About 75 grams. The water gives 100 times 60, which is 6,000 calories as it cools to 0. Dividing 6,000 by 80 gives 75 grams.
items.why: A strong answer works out the heat the katori can give, then divides by the heat needed for each gram. Real cubes melt a little less, since some heat is lost.

It admits that Sreedevi is right too, since an open field loses heat to the sky far faster than a closed shed can be warmed. items.p: Draw two small graphs of temperature through a day and a night. One is for a town by the sea, and one is for a town in the middle of a desert.
items.a: The sea town graph is a gentle wave with a small gap between its highest and lowest points. The desert town graph is a steep wave with a big gap, hot by day and cold by night.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a smaller swing for the sea town, and says that the sea holds a lot of heat and changes slowly.

items.p: Label this heating curve of ice being warmed until the water boils: ice warming, ice melting, water warming, water boiling.
items.a: Ice warming is the sloping line up to 0. Ice melting is the first flat part at 0. Water warming is the long slope from 0 to 100. Water boiling is the second flat part at 100.
items.why: The two flat parts are where the heat changes the state and not the temperature.

items.p: A 100-metre steel bridge grows about 4 centimetres when it warms by 30 degrees. About how much would it grow if it warmed by 15 degrees?
opts: About 2 centimetres
About 8 centimetres
About 4 centimetres
items.why: Half as much warming gives about half as much growth. Half of 4 is 2. Picking 8 doubles instead of halving.

items.p: James Joule let falling weights turn a paddle in water, and the water got a little warmer. Why does this show that heat is not a fluid stored inside the water?
items.a: The paddle was not letting any stored fluid out of the water. The movement of the paddle made the water warm. Doing more work made more heat, with no limit to it. So heat can come from movement itself.
items.why: A strong answer says that movement turned into heat, and that a fixed store would eventually run out.

items.p: At absolute zero, all the particles of a thing stop moving completely.
items.why: False. Quantum physics says that particles keep a tiny amount of movement even at absolute zero. They move as little as the rules allow.

items.p: A child tests which warms faster in the sun. She puts a thick brick in full sun and a thin steel plate in the shade. What is wrong with her test?
opts: She changed two things at once, the material and the place, so she cannot tell which caused the difference
Bricks cannot be warmed by the Sun
Steel plates should always be in the shade
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing. Here the material, the thickness and the sunshine all differ.

applications: Hot water bottles and water-filled heat packs keep a bed warm for hours, because water holds so much heat.
Passive solar buildings and greenhouses use drums or tanks of water, or thick stone walls, to soak up the day's sun and give it back at night.
Cars have radiators full of water and coolant to carry heat away from the engine, because water takes up a lot of heat.
Cooks choose pans by how they hold heat: a thick iron tawa stays hot for dosas, and a thin aluminium pan heats quickly.
Calorie labels on food packets tell us the heat energy in food, found by burning food in a sealed device, as in the groundnut test.
Weather forecasters use the sea's slow warming to explain why coastal towns have milder temperatures than inland ones, and why the monsoon starts.
Railways and bridges are built with expansion gaps, so that hot days do not bend the steel.
Steam engines and the steam in a pressure cooker work because boiling water stores a lot of hidden heat that steam gives back.
A clay matka or a wet cloth cools water by evaporation, without a fridge or any electricity.
Doctors use the fact that sweat cools us when they check for fever and heat stroke, and tell people to drink water in hot weather.

open_questions.q: Exactly why does water hold so much heat?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that links between water particles take in heat, but working out the exact number from first principles is still hard.

open_questions.q: Is there a hottest possible temperature?
open_questions.why_open: Coldest is clear: absolute zero. Nobody knows if hot has a limit, because at extreme temperatures the known laws of physics stop working.

open_questions.q: Why does water shrink as it cools to 4 °C and then expand again?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have good ideas about how the water particles arrange themselves, but the full reason is still being debated.

open_questions.q: How do living cells sense heat and cold?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists found special gates in cells that open at certain temperatures, work that won a Nobel Prize in 2021. How the whole body turns them into feelings of warm and cold is not fully understood.

open_questions.q: Does a black hole have a temperature?
open_questions.why_open: Stephen Hawking calculated in 1974 that a black hole should glow very faintly, like a warm object. Nobody has measured it, and nobody is sure how it works.

open_questions.q: How hot was the very early universe, and what was it made of?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists think the universe began extremely hot, and that matter was a soup of tiny particles for a moment. They study it by smashing nuclei together, but many questions remain.

maths.problem: In the Oil and Water test, the oil went from 29 °C to 60 °C and the water from 29 °C to 47 °C. How many degrees did each rise? How many more degrees did the oil rise?
maths.answer: The oil rose 31 degrees. The water rose 18 degrees. The oil rose 13 degrees more.
maths.explain: 60 minus 29 is 31. 47 minus 29 is 18. 31 minus 18 is 13. The oil, which needs less heat for each degree, rose by more.
maths.context: This is about the Oil and Water test, where oil and water stood in the same hot bath.
maths.why_maths: Taking each start from its end shows how far each liquid rose, so you can compare them fairly.

chart.title: Oil and Water: temperature after 12 minutes

maths.problem: A grown-up warms 250 grams of water from 30 °C to 70 °C. Water needs 1 calorie for each gram and each degree. How many calories does it take? How many kilocalories is that?
maths.explain: The rise is 70 minus 30, which is 40 degrees. 250 times 40 is 10,000. A kilocalorie is 1,000 calories, so 10,000 divided by 1,000 is 10 kilocalories.
maths.why_maths: Heat needed is the amount times the rise, so multiplying tells you how much heat to supply before you start.

maths.problem: A litre of water has a mass of 1,000 grams. How many calories does it take to warm 1 litre of water from 28 °C to 100 °C? One chapati has about 100 kilocalories. Is that enough?
maths.answer: 72,000 calories, which is 72 kilocalories. Yes, one chapati has enough.
maths.explain: The rise is 100 minus 28, which is 72 degrees. 1,000 times 72 is 72,000 calories. 72,000 divided by 1,000 is 72 kilocalories. 72 is less than 100, so one chapati holds enough heat.
maths.why_maths: Changing between calories and kilocalories lets you compare the heat for water with the heat in a food.

maths.problem: Meera mixes 1 litre of water at 80 °C with 3 litres of water at 20 °C. Work out the temperature of the mix.
maths.explain: 1 litre times 80 is 80. 3 litres times 20 is 60. 80 plus 60 is 140. There are 4 litres in all. 140 divided by 4 is 35.
maths.why_maths: Sharing the total heat over the total water gives the temperature where the mix settles.

maths.problem: In the Oil and Water test, oil needs about half as much heat as water for each degree. 100 grams of water warmed by 10 degrees needs 1,000 calories. How much heat does 100 grams of oil need for the same 10 degrees? What would 100 grams of oil warmed by 20 degrees need?
maths.answer: 500 calories for 10 degrees. 1,000 calories for 20 degrees.
maths.explain: Half of 1,000 is 500. For 20 degrees, double the 10 degrees: 500 times 2 is 1,000. So the oil warmed by 20 degrees needs the same heat as the water warmed by 10.
maths.context: This is about the Oil and Water test, and how much heat each liquid needed.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the heat for two materials as a ratio shows why the same heat warms the oil by twice as many degrees.

maths.problem: In the Stuck at Zero test, a child read the thermometer every 2 minutes: 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 5, 10. Look at the line graph. For how many minutes did the reading stay at about 0? At which minute did it first go above 1?
maths.answer: It stayed at about 0 for 10 minutes. It first went above 1 at minute 14.
maths.explain: The readings are at minutes 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16. The first six readings, from minute 0 to minute 10, are 0. At minute 12 the reading is 1. At minute 14 it is 5, the first number above 1.
maths.context: This is about the Stuck at Zero test, where a thermometer sat in melting ice.
maths.why_maths: A line graph makes the flat part easy to see, so you can find how long the ice took to melt.

maths.problem: An ice cube from the freezer is at minus 18 °C. By how many degrees must it warm before it starts to melt? And by how many degrees from minus 18 to the boiling point of water, 100 °C?
maths.answer: It must warm by 18 degrees to start melting. From minus 18 to 100 is 118 degrees.
maths.explain: From minus 18 up to 0 is 18 steps. From 0 up to 100 is 100 steps. 18 plus 100 is 118.
maths.why_maths: Counting up through zero shows how far ice has to travel on a thermometer before it starts to melt.

maths.problem: A 100-metre steel bridge grows about 4 centimetres when it warms by 30 degrees. About how much does it grow when it warms by 15 degrees? And by 60 degrees?
maths.answer: About 2 centimetres for 15 degrees. About 8 centimetres for 60 degrees.
maths.explain: 15 degrees is half of 30, so the growth is half of 4, which is 2. 60 degrees is double 30, so the growth is double 4, which is 8.
maths.why_maths: The growth goes up evenly with the warming, so doubling and halving let you predict a bridge's growth without measuring it.

maths.problem: The Katori and the Bowl test: the katori held 100 grams of water at 60 °C. The bowl held 1,000 grams at 40 °C. Cooling to 0 °C, which would give out more calories? By how many calories?
maths.answer: The bowl gives out more, by 34,000 calories.
maths.explain: The katori gives 100 times 60, which is 6,000 calories. The bowl gives 1,000 times 40, which is 40,000 calories. 40,000 minus 6,000 is 34,000.
maths.context: This is about the Katori and the Bowl test, where a katori of hot water and a bowl of warm water melted ice.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the amount by the temperature shows that a cooler bowl can hold far more heat, which explains the melted ice.

roots.context: We have measured how fast oil and water warm, and watched ice melt without a change in temperature. Now we ask what this tells us about thermometers, about our own bodies and about the world.

deep_truth.truth: The oil and the water sat in the same bath, and the oil ended up much hotter. A thermometer does not count the heat that went in. It shows how that one material answered the heat. So a temperature tells you about the stuff as well as the heat.
deep_truth.habit: We read a temperature as if it were an amount of heat, as in 'it is hotter, so it has more heat'. But the same heat gives a different temperature in different stuff, and the same temperature can hide very different amounts of heat.
deep_truth.evidence: In Oil and Water in a Warm Bath, both tumblers stood in the same bath. In a typical test the oil warmed by about twice as many degrees as the water. In the ice test, a small katori of water at 60 degrees melted less ice than a big bowl at 40.

three.who_am_i: You are about two thirds water, so your body warms and cools slowly. That helps to keep your inside near 37 degrees on a hot day and on a cool night.
three.what_is_life: A lizard takes in the sun's heat on a warm rock, and a hen makes her own. Water inside every living cell helps all of them keep their heat steady.
three.what_is_this_world: The seas hold so much heat that they steady the weather for whole countries. The Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea keep India's coasts milder than the plains far from them.

roots.thread: Heat is one thing, energy, but every kind of stuff takes it in in its own way. Oil takes it in mostly as faster movement, so it warms quickly. Water also spreads it into spinning, wobbling and stretching, so it warms slowly. The same heat meets many materials and shows up as many different temperatures. A warm sea, a hot sand dune and a 37-degree body are all the same energy, meeting different stuff.

science.text: Water has one of the highest specific heats of any common liquid. This is why seas steady the weather of coasts.
Exactly why water holds so much heat, and why it has dozens of other unusual properties, is still being worked out.

other_view.view: Temperature is a simple thing: the average energy of motion of the particles. It belongs to the heat alone. Oil and water follow the same rule. The water simply has more ways to store energy, so it needs more heat. Saying that temperature is partly about the stuff is a confusing way to put it.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if in a city flat, with the materials listed. Choices made: two thermometers are the one bought item, because the Oil and Water test needs both liquids read at the same time. With one thermometer, the unit says to do the test twice with a fresh bath. In the Oil and Water test, the bath is a wide pan at about 70 degrees, only 3 centimetres deep, so the steel tumblers rest on the bottom and do not float. The oil never goes on a flame and never exceeds about 70 degrees. Typical numbers, from working out the heat flow, are about 31 degrees of rise for the oil and 18 for the water in 12 minutes. The real ratio may be anywhere from 1.5 to 2.2, and the parent is told so. The Katori and the Bowl test uses 6 cubes in each, and the heat sums show that 100 grams of water at 60 degrees can melt only about 75 grams of ice. If the cubes are small, the parent is told to use more. Stuck at Zero uses a 2 litre warm bath so the bath stays warm, and the flat part lasts about 10 to 14 minutes. The balloon on a bottle needs a thin balloon that has been stretched first, and hot water that is not boiling, so the bottle does not soften. The groundnut test is done by a grown-up, with a steel plate, a bowl of water and an open window, and offers dry coconut for homes with a nut allergy. The water usually catches only a quarter to a third of the heat, and the unit says so. The sand and water project depends on sunshine. In the rains, the difference can be small, and the steps say to wait for a sunny day. The water is poured out at the end so mosquitoes cannot breed. Facts to verify before publishing: the Chennai and Jaisalmer day-and-night ranges (stated as about 8 to 10 and 15 or more), the Boomerang Nebula temperature (stated as reported), the several-trillion-degree figure (stated as reported), and Fahrenheit's mixing experiments as reported by Boerhaave (no numbers given). The spine is the Oil and Water test, the explanation cards, the Katori and the Bowl test, roots and the quiz.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, people thought that a thermometer told them how much heat a thing held. A hotter thing had more heat, and two things at the same temperature had the same amount. Early in the 1700s, the instrument-maker Daniel Fahrenheit mixed water and mercury at different temperatures. The mix did not land halfway, and the Dutch doctor Herman Boerhaave reported this puzzle. In the early 1760s, Joseph Black, a Scottish chemist and doctor at the University of Glasgow, thought hard about it. He argued that different materials need different amounts of heat to warm by the same number of degrees. He also saw that melting ice takes in a lot of heat while a thermometer in it stays still. So the amount of heat and the temperature are not the same thing. He gave them separate names and measured them separately. In the 1840s, James Joule showed that heat is energy, and that movement can turn into it.
how_we_found_out.who: Joseph Black, a Scottish chemist and doctor (1728 to 1799)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: A thermometer shows how much heat a thing holds, so things at the same temperature hold the same heat. Black showed that different materials, and different amounts, need different heat to change by the same number of degrees.
